title: Republican and Democratic coalitions put to the test in unusual elections on Tuesday
summary: Gov. Larry Rhoden faces outsider Toby Doeden in South Dakota's first-ever gubernatorial runoff while Georgia Democrats vie to replace Rep. David Scott.
story: Fox News anchor Bill Hemmer reports on Georgia’s 2026 gubernatorial primary and Trump-backed candidate Ed Gallrein's defeat of Thomas Massie in Kentucky on ‘Jesse Watters Primetime.’
Two races in politically disparate parts of the country set the stage for one of the most unusual split-screen election days of the year on Tuesday.
Rep. David Scott’s death in April at age 80 created a vacancy in a heavily blue district encompassing the southern and eastern Atlanta suburbs of Stockbridge, Conyers and Snellville.
With the general election ballot already decided, Tuesday’s contest will determine who will finish out Scott’s term. Scott was notably related by marriage to Braves slugger Hank Aaron.

Across the country in South Dakota, Republicans vying for the Mount Rushmore State’s safely red governor’s seat have created the state's first gubernatorial runoff between incumbent Gov. Larry Rhoden and self-made millionaire bitcoin investor Toby Doeden.
TRUMP’S GOP CLOUT FACES ARIZONA TEST WITH HOUSE MAJORITY, GOVERNOR’S RACE AT STAKE
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, left; the late Rep. David Scott, D-Ga., right. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images; Bill Clark/Getty Images)

Rhoden originally took the reins in Pierre after President Donald Trump chose former Gov. Kristi Noem to be Homeland Security secretary in his second term. He was unable to garner enough support in the June primary to secure the nomination outright in his first statewide election as governor.
South Dakota’s runoff is expected to be a classic establishment-versus-outsider race, with Rhoden heavily favored in the polls but Doeden hoping for a Sioux Falls-fueled upset.
Minnehaha County, home to Sioux Falls, is a key county to watch Tuesday after helping propel Doeden to a first-place finish in the June primary.
WATCH: LAWMAKERS REVEAL WHERE THEY STAND ON CONGRESSIONAL TERM LIMITS AFTER RECENT HEALTH SCARES

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks with the press during Education Secretary Linda McMahon’s "Returning Education to the States" tour on April 8, 2026, at McCrossan Boys Ranch in Sioux Falls, S.D. (Samantha Laurey / Argus Leader / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)
Pennington County, on the state’s western side, will also be closely watched after contributing to Doeden’s top finish in June.
In contrast to what is expected in Scott’s district in November, Republicans are heavily favored because South Dakota has not elected a Democratic governor since the 1970s.

Then-Gov. Richard Kneip served nearly two terms before President Jimmy Carter nominated him as ambassador to Singapore. Gov. Harvey Wollman completed the final six months of Kneip’s term, and is the state’s last Democrat to hold the office.
EX-NFL LINEBACKER POISED TO RETURN TO CONGRESS AFTER TEXAS RUNOFF WIN WITH JASMINE CROCKETT ENDORSEMENT
Shifting back to the Deep South, Georgia Democrats are expected to hold Scott’s seat in the fall by a wide margin.
Efforts to replace Scott grew in recent months, particularly among the party's progressive wing, as the 12-term, often-combative lawmaker drew increasing frustration from Democrats.
FROM LOCKER ROOMS TO CONGRESS, JAY FEELY THE LATEST ATHLETE SEEKING TO TAKE LESSONS ON LEADERSHIP TO CAPITOL HILL
A sign welcomes travelers to the Peach State at the I-20 East Welcome Center near Tallapoosa, Georgia, on October 3, 2022. (Charlie Creitz)
Last year, Scott made waves in Washington media when he shouted expletives at a Politico photographer as he was wheeled through the Capitol by staff.
"Who gave you the right to take my picture, a--hole," Scott shouted at photographer Francis Chung in late 2025.
That demeanor was similar to what led Everton Blair to launch his primary bid against Scott, in what his campaign page calls a "voice for a new generation."

Blair previously told Fox News Digital it was a run-in with Scott at a Gwinnett County town hall, where the lawmaker gave insufficient answers to questions and then reportedly became confrontational, that led him to explore a bid.

Blair had said he would "love to just hear a little bit more of the congressional and legislative strategy, congressman, that you have for this administration, particularly as it pertains to safeguarding federal funds," according to Semafor, when Scott replied "hold on," before becoming agitated:
"I don’t know who sent y’all, but we got these folks here who are providing answers. And I’m doing this. That’s what I’m doing," Scott said, according to the outlet.
Blair responded by launching a primary bid, while remarking to Fox News Digital at the time that two other elderly Democratic members had recently died in office "at a time when every vote counts."

The wave of millennial candidates seeking to replace aging Democrats was at the time dubbed the "Biden effect" — Democratic lawmakers retiring or facing potential primary challenges following the octogenarian Delawarean’s disastrous debate performance, which led to his decision to step aside for Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"Change can’t wait, and Democrats need a new bench of leaders who are committed to solving real problems for working people," Blair said in a previous press release.
Meanwhile, Scott’s daughter is hoping to replace her late father in Congress, remarking that she wants to continue his legacy.

"That is my thing, is to finish out his year strongly, make sure that this money gets down to the district, and just make sure the 13th district is taken care of, constituency-wise, and making sure the projects go into finalization," she told the Georgia Recorder, while adding she would retain her father’s staff locally and at the Capitol for added stability.

"[W]hen he first got into politics, I wasn’t even born, so I ran for some type of office or campaign every two years of my life, so this is just my norm, I’m just picking up where we left off with him," she told the outlet.
A third candidate, former Mississippi judge Carlos Moore, also criticized Rep. Scott’s tenure, telling the Mississippi Free Press he wants to be a "leader who actually shows up."
Moore had been suspended from the bench for one year in 2024 after a bar tribunal found he mishandled a wrongful death settlement, according to the outlet.

When asked by the press about the infraction, he pointed to Trump’s 34-count indictment in New York. He also pledged, if elected, to be a leader who understands "how to defend our democracy and Constitution" from the president.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The winner of Tuesday’s special elections will serve only until January.

Georgia state Rep. Jasmine Clark, D-Tucker, won the Democratic nomination for the full term earlier this year and is heavily favored against Republican Air Force veteran Jonathan Chavez in November. Trump lost the district by about 43 points in 2024.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Mamdani sparks fears of violence after doxing wealthy NYC property owners: 'Outright dangerous'
summary: The searchable database names affluent property owners who could face the proposed pied-à-terre tax, raising new privacy and security concerns.
story: An investigation into Zohran Mamdani's plans to enact rent controls on New York City real estate. Property owners and housing associations weight the real cost of the mayor’s radical agenda in Part 2 of

Mayor Zohran Mamdani opened a new front in his ongoing battle with New York City's wealthy after his administration published a searchable database identifying affluent property owners who could be subject to the city's proposed pied-à-terre tax, a move critics say could expose them to harassment and public safety risks.

The database, released by the city's Department of Finance, allows users to search properties and view the names and addresses of owners whose non-primary residences could be subject to the proposed tax. A spokesperson for the department said the publication of the property roll was required by state law.

"As per State law, a property roll was released for public inspection. From this list, DOF will identify properties that may be subject to the new non-primary residence property surcharge," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

A person familiar with the process, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said the city has publicly released similar property tax rolls every year for many years in accordance with New York state law. The person said new taxes and surcharges follow the same process: The state passes legislation, a public property roll is published, and the Department of Finance identifies the properties subject to the levy using criteria established by the state.
MAMDANI'S RENT FREEZE, TAX HIKES A 'ONE-TWO WEALTH DESTRUCTION PUNCH,' ECONOMISTS WARN
Manhattan attracted the nation's most new tax filers between 2022 and 2023 yet still saw a sharp decline in reported income as wealthy residents left. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

However, critics argue the database goes well beyond traditional public records by compiling the names and addresses of affluent property owners into a single, easily searchable location, potentially creating new privacy and security risks. The debate carries added weight in America's largest city, where public safety remains a persistent political issue and affluent residents have long cited crime as a top concern.

While property ownership records have long been public, opponents say the city's decision to aggregate them into a dedicated database could make wealthy homeowners more vulnerable to harassment and potential violence. City Hall has defended the database as a transparency tool designed to help property owners determine whether they could be affected by the proposed tax and understand how to seek an exemption.

"Nobody wants this database more than Mamdani’s band of communist social media agitators salivating to harass Americans at every turn," "Ruthless" podcast co-host John Ashbrook warned, pointing out the database could easily become a tool for Mamdani’s online supporters to target landlords and other property owners.
"They attack anybody who questions his decisions, and there’s no question they’ll harass every New Yorker who provides housing for a living," he continued.

A masked demonstrator carries a flag during a "Nakba 78" anti-Israel protest march in Manhattan on May 15, 2026, in New York City. He wears a hoodie marked "North American Connelly Association," a reference to an IRA group. (Michael Dorgan/Fox News Digital)

Meanwhile, the Real Estate Board of New York President James Whelan argued that the database also illustrates how broadly the proposed tax could reach beyond the ultra-wealthy residents its supporters have emphasized. Although Mamdani initially promoted the proposal as a tax on secondary homes worth more than $5 million and owned by the "ultra-wealthy and global elites," the final rules use different Department of Finance valuation thresholds depending on the type of property. According to the New York Post, over 960,000 residences could be listed in the database, which makes it possible to search and download property owners’ information, including their names and addresses.

"By publishing a database of properties that might be subject to this tax before the tax has even been enacted, City Hall has only added to the confusion surrounding this proposal," Whelan told Fox News Digital.

"What this database really demonstrates is that the second-home tax is far broader and more complicated than its supporters have suggested," he continued. "Policymakers should take a hard look at the many homeowners who could be swept in despite not fitting the profile of the ultra-wealthy residents this tax was supposedly designed to target."
MAMDANI THANKS SAME BILLIONAIRE HE TARGETED IN TAX VIDEO FOR NYPD MONEY
The database marks the latest flashpoint in Mamdani's increasingly contentious relationship with the city's wealthiest residents.

Earlier this year, the mayor stood outside Citadel founder Ken Griffin's 24,000-square-foot Central Park South penthouse, purchased for a record $238 million, to promote his proposal to raise taxes on second homes worth more than $5 million after previously criticizing the billionaire hedge fund manager over his personal wealth. The video singled out Griffin by name.
Griffin later called the video "creepy and weird," arguing it put him in harm's way because it highlighted his residence while promoting higher taxes on the wealthy.

Longtime Republican strategist Colin Reed argued that the database and Mamdani’s broader rhetoric against wealthy New Yorkers could carry dangerous consequences amid heightened concerns about political violence.

"In this era of heightened political violence, this type of inflammatory and divisive rhetoric is not only reckless, but outright dangerous, especially from a public official who not that long ago pledged to be a mayor for all New Yorkers," Reed told Fox News Digital.

"It’s bad enough that the mayor is demonizing success and upward mobility that has so long defined the American dream, and doing so within the city that has defined American capitalism," Reed continued. "But to do so by pitting various classes against one another is beneath the office he holds."
CHICAGO KNOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN KEN GRIFFIN TURNS ON A CITY, NOW MAMDANI MAY FIND OUT

The clash has also revived a broader debate over whether New York risks driving away the wealthy residents and businesses that have long underpinned its economy. Griffin, whose fortune Forbes estimates at roughly $50 billion, moved Citadel's global headquarters from Chicago to Miami in 2022 after years of criticizing the Windy City's tax policies, crime and business climate.

The departure marked Griffin's break from Chicago, where he built one of the world's largest hedge funds and helped cement the city as a global financial hub. He has since warned that New York could face similar consequences if policymakers pursue an agenda he believes is hostile to high-income residents and businesses.

On April 15, NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani posted a video outside Ken Griffin’s Manhattan penthouse promoting a new "tax-the-rich" policy. (Spencer Platt/Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg/Getty Images / Getty Images)

The latest controversy comes as business leaders closely watch whether New York's political climate is becoming less welcoming to the financial industry and wealthy taxpayers that have long anchored the city's economy.
At the center of the debate is whether the city can ask more of its wealthiest residents without weakening the tax base that helps fund municipal government.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office asking why the administration chose to publish the searchable database rather than notify affected property owners privately and whether it conducted a legal or privacy review before making the information available online. The office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: America's No. 1 state is crowned again — find out who's on top and where your state ranks this year
summary: Utah ranks as America's best state for a fourth straight year while Texas claims the No. 1 economy and South Dakota surges to the No. 2 spot.
story: At the Great American State Fair, Americans expressed cautious optimism about jobs and growth, but many told Fox News Digital values and leadership matter more than economic conditions at the ballot box.
Utah isn't giving up its crown.

The Beehive State came in at America's No. 1 state for the fourth consecutive year in U.S. News & World Report's 2026 Best States rankings, holding onto the top spot overall while Texas claimed the nation's highest-ranked economy.

The list points to a notable regional trend, with the Mountain West, Midwest and Sun Belt states claiming many of the country's highest overall rankings. Four of the top five states are located in the Mountain West or Upper Midwest, with Utah, South Dakota, Minnesota, North Dakota and Nebraska leading the overall rankings in order. New Hampshire, Idaho, Florida, Washington and Vermont rounded out the Top 10.

U.S. News Executive Chairman and CEO Eric Gertler said the results reflect what he called "a broader realignment of American economic growth," with states in the Midwest and South gaining ground as businesses and workers increasingly gravitate toward faster-growing, lower-cost regions.

"States in the Midwest and South generally moved up the rankings, while several Northeastern states fell substantially, showing how human and financial capital are actively migrating away from high-cost areas into more affordable regions," Gertler told Fox News Digital.
THIS RED STATE IS STRENGTHENING ITS GRIP AS AMERICA'S NEXT ECONOMIC HEAVYWEIGHT

Texas climbed to the No. 1 spot in the economy category after the Lone Star State ranking the year prior. U.S. News credited the state with leading the nation in job growth while posting among the country's strongest performances in GDP growth, net migration and youth population growth.

South Dakota, meanwhile, posted one of the year's biggest gains, climbing from No. 8 overall to No. 2, while North Dakota jumped from No. 12 to No. 4, driven by improvements in health care, education, fiscal stability and economic performance.
Gertler described 2026 as the "Year of the Midwest," pointing to the Dakotas' rapid ascent as evidence of a broader shift in economic momentum.
"Low cost of living combined with strategic manufacturing investments are making these states prime destinations for young workers and expanding businesses," Gertler said.
BILLIONS IN TAXPAYER INCOME ARE LEAVING TWO ICONIC STATES — AS A NEW ECONOMIC MAP EMERGES
Visitors hike along a trail in Bryce Canyon National Park in Tropic, Utah, on March 9, 2026. (Photo by Michael Yanow/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Utah, meanwhile, maintained its dominance by placing in the Top 10 across five of the report's eight major categories, including No. 2 in the economy and fiscal stability and No. 4 in infrastructure.
Gertler attributed Utah's sustained success to the state's overall consistency.
"Utah's No. 1 ranking comes down to consistency," he said, pointing to the state's strong economy, fiscal stability and education system, along with its young and growing workforce.
One of the report's most striking findings was that the nation's top-ranked state also placed 48th in natural environment, underscoring that no single category determines the overall standings.

No state dominated every category. Colorado climbed to No. 1 in education, Hawaii topped the nation in health care, Nevada ranked first in infrastructure, Wyoming led in fiscal stability, New Hampshire earned the highest marks in crime and corrections, Vermont ranked first in opportunity and Hawaii also claimed the top spot in natural environment.
The Beehive State finished in the Top 10 across five of the report's eight major categories, helping it retain the nation's highest overall ranking. (George Rose/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Among the nation's largest states, Florida was the only one to crack the overall Top 10, finishing eighth. Texas paired its top-ranked economy with continued population and job growth, while California and New York did not finish among the top 10 overall.

The annual U.S. News Best States rankings compare all 50 states across eight categories that include the economy, education, healthcare, infrastructure, opportunity, fiscal stability, crime and corrections, and natural environment.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Dems clash over AIPAC money, ‘ogre’ attack and electability during crucial Senate debate
summary: El-Sayed refused to apoelogize for the “ogre on a pike" remark that drew backlash from fellow Democrats, while Haley Stevens slammed him over his unreleased tax returns and roughly $300k in outside income.
story: Rep. Hillary Scholten accused Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed of making sexist remarks about female Democrats, including Rep. Haley Stevens and Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
The battle between the Democratic Party's far-left flank and establishment wing spilled onto the stage Monday night during battleground Michigan's fiery Senate debate.

The debate took place one week ahead of the pair’s Aug. 4 primary battle, with both candidates using the final face-off to sharpen their competing arguments over who could best represent Michigan — and defeat Republican candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers, in the November 3 general election.

During Monday night's clash of the Democratic Party's competing wings, El-Sayed doubled down on his "ogre on a pike" remark and declined to apologize, but clarified it was not specifically directed at Stevens but rather a different moderate Democrat in Congress. Meanwhile, El-Sayed also repeated his attacks on pro-Israel and corporate spending supporting Stevens, while he also rejected the "socialist" label some have given him, describing himself as a "just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works."

Stevens, on the other hand, questioned what El-Sayed was "hiding" by not releasing his full tax returns, an attack she carried over from the pair's first one-on-one debate earlier this month, and portrayed his rhetoric, outside income and national political ambitions as potential general-election liabilities when it came to taking on Rogers and trying to win the U.S. Senate seat they are vying for.
SWING-STATE POLL SPELLS TROUBLE FOR FAR LEFT AS SCHUMER-BACKED CANDIDATE DOMINATES WITH CRITICAL VOTING BLOCS

Retiring Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., has abandoned his neutrality in Michigan's high-stakes Democratic Senate primary, backing U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, pictured left, as party leaders rally to stop progressive rival Abdul El-Sayed, pictured right, from winning the nomination. (AP Photo/Kristen Norman)
El-Sayed confirms Fetterman was the ‘ogre,’ declines to apologize

El-Sayed stood by the substance of his controversial "ogre on a pike" remark when pressed by the moderator about whether he regretted the rhetoric, which earned him backlash from his own party, but clarified it was about Sen. John Fetterman, D-Penn., not Stevens as some had speculated.
"I was referring to a guy named John Fetterman," El-Sayed said, accusing the Pennsylvania Democrat of getting elected on one set of values before "completely throwing those values in the mud."

El-Sayed did not apologize for or retract the metaphor. Instead, he argued that he had previously pushed back against unkind treatment of Stevens, including after she was booed at a Michigan Democratic Party convention.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: THE REPUBLICAN-LED VOTE THAT REVEALED DEMOCRATS' NEW DIVIDE ON ISRAEL
Stevens later offered a pointed response: "Thank you for clarifying that you didn’t call me an ogre."
U.S. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters outside the Senate Chamber during votes on Nov. 10, 2025 on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

The controversy stemmed from comments El-Sayed made during a recent Zoom meeting with donors, Politico reported, adding that El-Sayed was discussing how to use his victory in Michigan’s upcoming Aug. 4 primary and the November election to build a national platform to move the Democratic Party further left and support future primary challenges, such as against Fetterman.

"Ideally, you put one ogre on a pike, and then everyone else gets the message," El-Sayed said, according to audio obtained by Politico. El-Sayed did not name Stevens in the recording; however, some Democrats interpreted the remark as referring to her. Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., who has endorsed Stevens, called the remark a "violent, vulgar" threat and said candidates should be working to lower the political temperature.

Neera Tanden, a former Biden administration official who leads the left-wing think tank the Center for American Progress, connected the remark to broader accusations of sexism that have roiled the primary.
"Calling your female opponent an ogre you want to put on a pike is not beating the rap that this race has some serious sexism," Tanden wrote on X.
AIPAC money and Israel fuel fierce confrontations

Tens of millions of dollars in outside spending supporting Stevens became a central flashpoint, with the moderator repeatedly pressing the congresswoman on whether pro-Israel groups would influence her conduct in office.

Asked whether the more than $46 million in AIPAC-related spending cited by the moderator should concern voters that she would do the group’s "bidding," Stevens responded, "Absolutely not," and defended her support for a two-state solution.
"I have been very clear, consistent and transparent," Stevens said. "I want to see long-term peace."
NEW YORK TIMES RAISES EYEBROWS BY REFERRING TO AIPAC AS 'HARD-RIGHT' PRO-ISRAEL GROUP
El-Sayed argued that the spending exposed a fundamental difference between the candidates, claiming AIPAC-backed groups supported Stevens because "they know that she’ll be a reliable vote."
"The difference between us is $46 million of AIPAC spending," El-Sayed said. "They’ve set a record in this race to help elect my opponent."

He then tied that spending directly to Stevens’ recent vote supporting additional aid to Israel, accusing the Israeli government of working to "foreclose on the possibility of Palestinian self-determination."

"I want your tax dollars spent in Michigan to provide schools in Michigan, to build healthcare in Michigan, to build roads in Michigan," El-Sayed said. "And I think that money sent over there to kill kids and women is the worst use of our tax dollars. And yet that’s exactly what $46 million in spending will buy you."
El-Sayed later added that the United States should not be "fighting stupid wars that AIPAC wants us to fight in the first place."
Stevens countered that outside groups were supporting both campaigns and accused El-Sayed of benefiting from a super PAC funded in part by his father-in-law.
Stevens presses El-Sayed over unreleased tax returns and outside income

Stevens continued to question El-Sayed’s financial transparency, as she did in their debate earlier this month, accusing him of refusing to release his full tax returns while earning approximately $300,000 in outside income.
"You have not released your full tax returns — $300,000 in other income while you sat in the podcast chair, and you hawked junk healthcare cures that RFK Jr. would thumbs up," Stevens charged.

"You talk about getting money out of politics and putting money in people’s pockets, but still, no one knows who’s putting the money in your pocket," she added, continuing a debate-long effort to portray El-Sayed as more interested in podcasts, high-profile political allies and building his national celebrity than doing the unglamorous work of representing Michigan.
El-Sayed responded that he had released his required financial disclosures, drawing a distinction between those filings and the full tax returns Stevens had demanded.

"We released all of our financial disclosures," El-Sayed said, calling the issue "a distraction" before turning the transparency argument back on Stevens and questioning the donors behind outside organizations supporting her campaign.
Stevens described herself as "the only non-millionaire in this race" and argued that El-Sayed’s finances could give Republicans additional material to use against him in November.
"What are the Republicans going to uncover in the general election that they will use against him?" she asked.
El-Sayed brands the Senate filibuster ‘anti-democratic’
Asked to identify the most important thing Senate Democrats were failing to do, El-Sayed immediately targeted the legislative filibuster and the 60-vote threshold it often imposes.
"I oppose the filibuster," El-Sayed said. "I think the filibuster has been anti-democratic for a lot of reasons."
TRUMP DEMANDS THUNE KEEP SENATE IN SESSION UNTIL SAVE AMERICA ACT PASSES

The U.S. Capitol dome is illuminated as the House of Representatives returns to Washington to vote to reopen the government on Wednesday, November 12, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

El-Sayed argued that eliminating the filibuster would help Democrats pass the PRO Act, which would expand union-organizing and collective-bargaining protections, impose tougher penalties for labor-law violations and override state right-to-work restrictions on mandatory union fees. He said it could also clear a path for stronger antitrust enforcement, which El-Sayed said needs to be more aggressive, as well as a wealth tax on billionaires and Medicare for All.
"Right now, the biggest risks to our democracy are the filibuster — it’s anti-democratic in the Senate — and money in politics," he said.
ICE clash exposes sharp divide between the Democratic rivals

The candidates also battled over the future of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with Stevens calling ICE a "rogue agency" while El-Sayed labeled it "tyrannical" and called for abolishing it altogether.

Stevens said she was leading an effort in Congress to redirect $70 billion allocated to ICE toward healthcare, food assistance and local communities. "Not a penny more for this rogue agency that is wreaking havoc," Stevens said, accusing ICE of abusing its power and frightening immigrant families.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent stands before a large American flag. ICE is expected to ramp up enforcement operations following the Supreme Court's decision allowing the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for more than 300,000 Haitians. (Photo by Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)
Meanwhile, El-Sayed accused Stevens of hypocrisy, alleging that she had previously voted four times to increase ICE funding and had praised its personnel.
"I’ve said that we need to abolish ICE," El-Sayed said. "ICE is about normalizing paramilitary force on our streets."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Pressed on whether the phrase "abolish ICE" carried the same political baggage as "defund the police," El-Sayed argued that the government could still enforce immigration laws and secure the southern border through a replacement agency.
He escalated the criticism moments later, calling ICE "a tyrannical agency."
"I think there is no way to get past that except to undo the agency and then build from scratch," El-Sayed said.
Stevens rejected his approach as focused more on rhetoric than governing.
"Complaints and slogans aren’t solutions," she said, pointing to her visit to an ICE detention facility and her efforts to change the agency through Congress.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Biden's classified docs narrative crumbles amid release of ghostwriter tapes: 'Be careful'
summary: Over 2.5 hours of recordings between Joe Biden and memoir ghostwriter Mark Zwonitzer reveal halting speech and memory struggles during the 2017 sessions.
story: New recordings between Joe Biden and memoir ghostwriter Mark Zwonitzer have been released. In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall two economic advisers. (Credit: The Oversight Project)

Former President Joe Biden's recordings from interviews with his memoir ghostwriter — obtained during special counsel Robert Hur's classified documents investigation — have been released to the public.
After a months-long fight from Biden’s attorneys to block the release of the tape, they abandoned their lawsuit calling for a dismissal Friday, in which a judge accepted Monday.

The plaintiff, Mike Howell formerly with conservative think tank Heritage Foundation and now at Oversight Project, has fought for more than two years to obtain the materials through FOIA requests, arguing that the public has an interest in reviewing the recordings and transcripts on which Hur based his decision.
BIDEN'S HUR INTERVIEW TAPES COULD NOW GO PUBLIC AFTER HIS ATTORNEYS WAVE WHITE FLAG
Former President Biden was dogged throughout his term by rumors of his purported cognitive decline. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

The Oversight Project published hours of recordings from Biden's 2016 and 2017 conversations with his "Promise Me, Dad" ghostwriter, Mark Zwonitzer, in which the then-former vice president frequently pauses, speaks haltingly and struggles to recall events — reinforcing Special Counsel Robert Hur's characterization in his report.

"Joe Biden didn’t want these tapes to come out. But now they have — after two years of painful delay. There is no joy in Bidenville today. Robert Hur’s and Merrick Garland’s decision to give Biden a free pass for keeping and disclosing classified information must now be reexamined from top to bottom," Oversight Project Vice President of Litigation Jeff Clark exclusively told Fox News Digital.
The House Judiciary Committee announced there were 2 hours and 45 minutes of recordings released.

Hur investigated Biden’s handling of classified documents dating from his time as vice president in the Obama administration and as a U.S. senator from Delaware. He declined to pursue criminal charges because he concluded prosecutors could not prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Biden willfully retained or disclosed the material.
HUNTER BIDEN RESURFACES IN LA, REACTS TO QUESTIONS ABOUT BIDEN TAPES, UFO FILES
US President Joe Biden speaks during a State of the Union address at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Feb. 7, 2023. (Nathan Howard/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
In his report, Hur wrote that Biden’s conversations were "painfully slow" and said Biden was "struggling to remember events and straining at times to read and relay his own notebook entries."
"Mr. Biden's memory was significantly limited, both during his recorded interviews with the ghostwriter in 2017 and in his interview with our office in 2023," wrote Hur.

He also said, in shocking reasoning for the lack of prosecution, that Biden could appear to a jury as a "sympathetic, well-meaning, elderly man with a poor memory" rather than an intentional violator of classified document laws.
The interview recordings show instances where Biden takes long pauses, forgets names, and can't recall specific days.
Biden warned Zwonitzer while discussing a 2014 Situation Room meeting, "Some of this may be classified, so be careful," and added, "I'm not sure. It isn't marked classified, but...."
In one instance, on April 24, 2017, Biden struggled to recall two economic advisers.
"I’ll think of his name," said Biden, and then, "I should write the names down because I keep forgetting them." A long pause follows before Zwonitzer says Alan Krueger’s name.
On the same day, Biden fails to recall where he was on a certain date, later remembering he was at a memorial for a fallen service member – and forgot his name.

"I think I went to that memorial service in Wilmington. It says [REDACTED] December the 4th, but I don't -- I know what this means. Memorial service -- [REDACTED] gets names really f---ed up," said Biden. "So it says memorial service for [REDACTED]. I don't think her name was [REDACTED]. Or I forget [REDACTED]."
Zwonitzer responded, "Okay," and Biden said he would "make a note of that too."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Then-Sen. Joe Biden delivered a fiery speech in 1989 calling on the H.W. Bush administration to launch an "international strike force" on narco-terrorists. (Cynthia Johnson/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"But at any rate, back to -- there was -- I had a meeting with Ron Klain, and I don't know when," Biden added.
Biden also appeared to struggle in recalling a lunch with former United States Secretary of the Treasury Larry Summers.
"When he, when he came to me — and I’ll get the date. Remind me when did Summers come to me to have lunch to — it was when I was thinking about running."
He later goes on to say, "Here’s what happened, before I forget. Don’t mind my train of thought. He also pledged to support me in 2016."
Fox News Digital reached out to the Office of Joe Biden for comment.
Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: Senate clears way for Trump's top spy as key anti-terror program remains in limbo
summary: Jay Clayton's Senate confirmation as DNI is set for Tuesday, potentially restarting the Section 702 FISA surveillance tool that went dark amid battles.
story: Chad Pergram reports from Capitol Hill, highlighting Democrats pressing Clayton on his stance regarding 2020 election claims and his delayed testimony, a move orchestrated by President Donald Trump over the SAVE America Act.

President Donald Trump’s pick to run the nation’s intelligence agencies is one step closer to clinching the job, and puts the Senate ever-closer to jump-starting a key counter-terrorism tool in the process.

The Senate advanced Jay Clayton through a key hurdle Monday night to be the next Director of National Intelligence (DNI). It comes after former DNI Tulsi Gabbard’s sudden exit from the position to care for her cancer-stricken husband.

The largely partisan 51-43 vote to move Clayton, who formerly chaired the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) during Trump’s first term, comes after he narrowly squeaked out the Senate Intelligence Committee on a 9 to 8 vote.
TRUMP'S DNI PICK CLEARS KEY HURDLE, REVIVING PATH FOR NATION'S TOP ANTI-TERROR SURVEILLANCE PROGRAM

United States attorney for the Southern District of New York Jay Clayton, nominee to be director of national intelligence, testifies during his confirmation hearing with the Senate Intelligence Committee at the Dirksen Senate Office Building in Washington, D.C., on July 15, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., challenged Democrats to support Clayton during the broader, final vote, but expected them to resist as they have with several other Trump nominees through his second term.

"One might think that we'd be seeing some bipartisanship from Democrats on this nominee," Thune said. "But Democrats are playing the same partisan games with this qualified nominee as they have for so many of President Trump's picks."

"It's a funny thing because Democrats have made no secret of their disdain for the current acting Director of … National intelligence," he continued. "In fact, Democrats were so worked up over the president's temporary choice for this position, they allowed our nation's most important counterterrorism tool to go dark for the first time ever."
TRUMP CONCESSION BREATHES NEW LIFE INTO STALLED FISA SPY POWERS DEAL

The Senate will now vote on confirmation Tuesday, putting an end cap on an arduous process to replace Gabbard. When she announced her exit from the position, Trump hastily installed Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) Director Bill Pulte to lead the nation’s 18 intelligence agencies in the interim.

That came as the Senate was nearing a vote on a bipartisan deal to keep the nation’s top counter-terrorism tool, Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA), running ahead of its expiration.

But Democrats, who railed against Pulte and accused him of being an unqualified loyalist who would weaponize the intelligence community against the president’s enemies and try to dismantle it, walked away from the deal after Trump torpedoed Clayton’s previously scheduled confirmation hearing.
SPY LAW USED TO STOP TAYLOR SWIFT ATTACK TO LAPSE AS CONGRESS SKIPS TOWN, WORLD CUP NEARS

Acting Director of National Intelligence Bill Pulte attends a kick-off celebration for the "Great American State Fair" on the National Mall in Washington, DC, June 24, 2026. (Jemal COUNTESS / AFP via Getty Images)
Less than 24 hours before Clayton's penultimate test, Pulte announced on X that he had completed his fourth round of layoffs as DNI.

"Since becoming Acting Director of National Intelligence, our team has been smartly, and carefully, reducing the size of ODNI, re-focusing ODNI on national security, the law, and the statute," Pulte said. "As of this evening, we just finished a 4th round of thoughtful, measured layoffs. Thank you!"

The Section 702 program has since been steadily going dark, with new authorizations caught in a legal void until lawmakers reauthorize the program that has been used to thwart deadly terror attacks, including halting a mass-casualty terror plot at a Taylor Swift show in Vienna, Austria.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Last week, only Republicans on the panel voted Clayton out of committee after he failed to satisfy Senate Democrats’ questioning on who won the 2020 election, his knowledge of Gabbard’s raid on the Fulton County, Georgia election offices, and subpoenas against New York Times reporters that his were submitted by him in his role as the top prosecutor in New York’s Southern District.
Those subpoenas were voluntarily withdrawn by the Department of Justice last week, two days after Clayton was confirmed by the panel.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Summer School: Republicans' crusade to teach voters the 'New Math' on the 'commie caucus'
summary: House Republicans hope Democrats' far-left candidates will help the GOP maintain its narrow House majority heading into the midterm elections.
story: Chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports as Congress prepares for its August recess.
The House is gone. But the campaign is on.
"We're going to have a lot to talk about during this break," said House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La. "The contrast on the ballot this November between communism and freedom."

School is out for the summer in the House until August 31. But Republicans envision a version of summer school for the voters. They intend to educate people about Democratic candidates who are veering to the left.
"The reality is that the communist caucus, the commie caucus is coming to Congress," claimed Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOUSE'S FINAL SPRINT PUTS SAVE AMERICA ACT AND IRAN FUNDING IN PLAY
The House might be a lost cause for Republicans, but their summer campaign to educate voters on the Democrats' insurgent left flank has just begun. (Emma Woodhead/Fox News Digital)

Republicans hope to cling to their narrow House majority by distinguishing themselves from Democrats – and noting how Democrats tapped far-left candidates in New York City and even Colorado. These "Democratic Socialists of America" candidates will undoubtedly prevail in their districts. But Republicans believe that left-wing Democrats freak out independents and mainstream Democrats. The GOP is banking on that as an insurance policy to maintain control of the House.

House Republicans also enjoyed some relative success last week for the first time in months. The GOP advanced a host of bills important to them. And, simultaneously got Democrats on the record about bills which Republicans think they can boomerang against their adversaries this fall.

"They have to answer for why they voted against funding our troops, against funding the government, against common sense policies like voter ID and proof of citizenship," said House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La.

"They have to answer for why they voted against funding our troops, against funding the government, against common sense policies like voter ID and proof of citizenship," House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., said of the opposition. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The House approved a plan barring stock trades by Members, 232-198. Only 13 Democrats voted yes compared to all Republicans. But the GOP tacked on a voter ID mandate. Democrats argue that provision transformed a once bipartisan issue into a GOP political wedge.

"I proudly voted no because we are not going to sabotage mail-in voting in this country. And we're not going to fall for that kind of bait-and-switch tactic here," fumed Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y.
Democrats have long campaigned on affordability.
"Today, prices are up over 25 cents a gallon above $4 a gallon in my region," said Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon, D-Pa.
SUCCESSION: WHY CONGRESS HAS NO CLEAR PLAN WHEN LAWMAKERS CAN’T SERVE
President Donald Trump has now paused the air campaign against Iran after two weeks of consecutive bombing. But the war in Iran presents Democrats with a political opening.
"Will Democrats recalibrate their message on Iran? Will we see ads on Iran going into the midterms?" yours truly asked House Minority Leader Jeffries, D-N.Y.
"We don't have to recalibrate our message. We've been opposed to Donald Trump's reckless and costly war of choice in the Middle East from the very beginning," replied Jeffries.
There was a split decision on Capitol Hill last week. The House voted to shackle the president on Iran war powers. Four Republicans defected and sided with Democrats.
"He ran on no new wars," said Rep. Becca Balint, D-Vt. "He's making the case for us. He hit voters over and over and over with this promise. And then he did the exact opposite."
President Trump has paused the air campaign against Iran after weeks of regular bombing. (CENTCOM)
Still, the president’s allies claimed that the vote undercuts American forces in harm’s way.
"To belittle this mission is to belittle and demean the very service these members who gave their lives," said House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla.
A couple of hours later, the Senate rejected the House’s rebuke of the President.
"I think Democrats have taken that tack from the start," said Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., of the Democrats hoping to cut off the Iran operation.
"It wouldn't have passed if it wasn't for Republicans in the House," yours truly pointed out.
"A few Republicans," conceded Hoeven. "But I think there's strong support in our party (for the President)."
That’s ultimately why the Senate defeated its Iran measure. Some GOPers argued that the U.S. has Iran on the ropes.

"Last time I checked, we've wiped these b------s out. An occasional missile strike and boats in the Strait (of Hormuz). That's not military strength. Those are the flailings of a failing empire," declared Sen. Tim Sheehy, R-Mont.
HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS
But Senate Democrats chided Republicans for not intervening in the conflict.

"Every time Republicans oppose our war powers resolution and vote against ending this war, they lose the faith of the American people," said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y. "Senate Republicans need to wake up. Not next week. Not next month. Now."
Top Congressional GOP leaders say it’s not necessary for Congress to flex its war powers muscles.
"I don't think an AUMF (authorization for use of military force) is in order right now. I think we need to bring this to a resolution," said Johnson.
Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, is calling for "greater clarity" on the Iran conflict. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
However, some Republicans demand answers about the endgame.
"I think we need greater clarity there. I think Congress needs to exercise more of its powers here," said Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas.
Democrats may believe they have an advantage on Iran. But like Roy, they demand a plan.
"This whiplash policy in Iran is not good," said Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss., the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee. "You can't run a war at 2:00 in the morning on Twitter."
JOHNSON HAS THREE-WORD ANSWER ON WHETHER HOUSE WILL LEAVE EARLY
Despite their criticism, Democrats are vague about how they'd go about ending the war.
"We've got to figure that out. But Donald Trump got us into this mess," said Jeffries.
"But won't voters demand you guys to have a plan if you're going to win the majority, Mr. Leader?" I asked as Jeffries walked away.
I posed a similar question to Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., one of the most thoughtful Democrats on foreign policy and national security issues.
"We didn't start it," replied Coons.
"But don’t you have to have a plan if you're going to criticize the president on this?" I asked.
"I wouldn't have gotten into this war," said Coons.
Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., was more blunt – saying outright that he "wouldn't have gotten into this war." (Photo by Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The Pentagon is now running short on cash since the defense policy bill is stalled. That’s to say nothing of the budget resolution which could provide $95 billion to the Pentagon. Congressional approval to pay for the war could take months. Perhaps until December. That’s after the election. Democrats may want to see how they fare in the midterms before coughing up money for the military.
Midterm elections are often a referendum on the president.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

In 2006, Democrats flipped the House and Senate by campaigning on ending the unpopular war in Iraq. They had a plan to wind down the conflict. Eighteen years later, Democrats want to run on Iran in this fall’s midterms. But unlike 2006, they don’t seem to have a clear plan on how to end the conflict.
But they know who to blame: President Trump.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Wearable patch vibrates when danger is nearby
summary: NC State researchers built a solar-powered wearable patch with six sensors that vibrates against your skin using distinct haptic alerts for each hazard.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Your phone can warn you about bad weather or heavy traffic. However, some dangers cannot wait for you to notice a notification. A hazardous gas may already surround you. Contaminated water may look perfectly normal. By the time you unlock your phone and check an alert, you could have already spent valuable time near the threat.

Researchers at North Carolina State University have developed a wearable patch that takes the phone out of that warning process. The device detects environmental hazards, then vibrates directly against your skin.
Different vibration patterns tell you which hazard the patch detected. Meanwhile, a related version gives robots their own form of chemical awareness.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class "Sick of Spam?" has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
SELF-DRESSING CLOTHES COULD HELP OLDER ADULTS

Researchers developed a wearable patch that detects hazardous gases and water contaminants, then warns users with vibrations directly against the skin before they check a phone. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A wearable warning you can feel immediately

The square patch is slightly smaller than a driver's license. That makes it compact enough to attach to clothing or place directly against the skin. Inside, a microcontroller acts as the patch's brain. A small battery powers the system. Six sensors monitor the surrounding environment for potential hazards.

The researchers designed the sensors to detect threats in the air and contaminants in water. Examples include dangerous gases and heavy metals. Once the patch detects a hazard, a tiny actuator creates a vibration against your skin. That physical alert could be harder to overlook than another phone notification.

"If you're coming into contact with a hazardous substance, you need to know as quickly as possible," said Erim Uzunoğlu, the paper's first author and a Ph.D. student at NC State. The research appears in the scientific journal Device.
Why the patch uses vibrations instead of phone alerts

Environmental sensors already exist. Many can send a warning to your smartphone. However, that approach depends on you noticing the alert. Your phone could be in a pocket, buried in a bag or silenced during work.

A physical vibration removes that extra step. The warning reaches your body as soon as the sensor detects a potential threat. Still, the researchers found that adding a small vibrating motor was not enough. The sensation had to feel strong and distinct without becoming uncomfortable.

To solve that problem, they created tiny textured surfaces between the motor and the skin. These surfaces resemble miniature patterns of raised bumps. By changing the size and spacing of the bumps, the team adjusted how each vibration felt. As a result, the alert became easier to notice. The design could prove helpful in loud environments where an audible alarm might disappear into the background.
Different vibration patterns identify each hazard

The patch does not use the same buzzing sensation for every warning. Instead, it produces a separate haptic sequence for each hazard. One pattern might signal a dangerous gas. Another could warn about a contaminant in water.

This creates a small tactile language between the patch and the person wearing it. Therefore, you may understand the type of threat without checking a display. In proof-of-concept testing, the patch successfully detected the targeted substances. It also triggered the appropriate vibration immediately.
However, people would need time to learn what each pattern means. Clear training would become especially important in workplaces where several hazards may be present.
Solar cells help extend the battery life

A wearable safety device offers little protection when its battery dies halfway through the day. To reduce that risk, the researchers placed thin-film photovoltaic cells on the patch's exterior. These cells collect solar energy while someone wears the device.

The solar cells work alongside the internal battery. At the same time, the sensors use relatively little power. During testing, that combination kept the device operating for around 24 hours. That running time could cover a full work shift. However, real-world performance would depend on sunlight, sensor activity and how someone wears the patch.
COULD A PAINT-ON ELECTRONIC TATTOO SPOT HEART ATTACKS?

A new wearable sensor uses distinct vibration patterns to alert users to environmental dangers, while a companion system gives robots the ability to detect chemical hazards. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Researchers give robots a chemical warning system

As the team developed the wearable patch, the researchers began considering another question. Could a robot use the same tactile warning system? That idea led to an electronic skin, also called e-skin.

The robotic version places the sensor patch over a piezoelectric layer. When the patch vibrates, that movement creates an electrical signal. The robot can read the signal and identify the vibration pattern. It can then respond to the detected hazard without waiting for a wireless message.

During testing, researchers placed the e-skin on quadrupedal robots. When the robots detected chemical hazards, they changed direction and followed a safer route. This system could help robots explore locations that may be unsafe for people. It could also let a machine respond when wireless connections become unreliable.
Why the robot e-skin could be important

Most robots rely heavily on cameras and digital instructions to understand their surroundings. Yet a camera cannot always identify a dangerous gas or invisible contaminant. The e-skin gives a robot another way to sense risk. More importantly, it turns the chemical warning into a physical signal within the robot's body.

That direct connection could support faster decisions. The robot would not need to transmit sensor data to a remote computer before responding. For example, a robot could inspect an industrial site while watching for leaks. It could then stop or change direction when it encounters a dangerous substance.
However, this work remains at the proof-of-concept stage. Researchers will need to test the system across harsher conditions before it can support high-risk missions.

Many experimental wearables rely on highly specialized components. Those custom parts can increase costs and slow production. In contrast, the researchers built most of this patch and e-skin with components that are already available. Only a few elements required custom engineering. That could make the technology easier to scale.

The sensor array is also modular. Developers could remove sensors that are unnecessary for a certain environment. They could then add sensors for hazards tied to a specific job or location. A water-quality worker would need a different setup than someone inspecting an area for chemical leaks.
What this means to you

You cannot buy this wearable hazard detection patch yet. Still, the research shows how safety alerts could move beyond screens and speakers. A vibration against your skin may reach you faster than a notification on your phone. That could become especially valuable when every second affects your exposure.

The technology may eventually help people who work near chemicals or inspect questionable water supplies. It could also support emergency teams entering places where the air may be unsafe. However, several questions remain. Researchers must determine how the patch performs after repeated wear and exposure to harsh conditions. They will also need to reduce false alarms and make each vibration easy to recognize. Comfort will play a role too. A safety patch only works when people are willing to wear it throughout the day.
NEW YORK SCHOOL DISTRICT TO DEPLOY HUMANOID ROBOT IN CLASSROOMS THIS FALL
Scientists at North Carolina State University created a smart patch that could help workers recognize dangerous chemicals through touch instead of smartphone notifications. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

A warning can only protect you when it reaches you in time. This wearable patch brings the alert directly to your skin instead of relying on a phone that you may never check. The separate vibration patterns are especially clever. They could tell you which danger is nearby before you even look at a screen. Meanwhile, the robot e-skin gives machines a physical way to recognize chemical threats and move away from them. That could eventually keep people farther from hazardous areas. The next challenge will be turning a successful laboratory prototype into something durable, comfortable and dependable enough for daily use.
Would you trust a vibration on your skin to tell you that the air you are breathing or the water near you has become dangerous? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: What your internet provider, websites and advertisers see
summary: Your internet provider, websites and advertisers can track your browsing activity even without you posting online. Here's how to limit what they see.
story: Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson lays out how to limit what health apps used by insurance companies can track about you, the user.
Most people assume that if they are not posting on social media or sharing personal information online, they are staying relatively private. Unfortunately, that isn't how today's internet works.

Every time you browse the web, multiple companies can collect information about you. Your internet provider can monitor certain parts of your online activity, websites can gather data about your visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles based on your browsing habits.
The good news? Knowing what others can see is the first step toward protecting your privacy.
AI WEARABLE WATCHES YOU TO PREDICT WHAT YOU NEED
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
Internet providers, websites and advertisers can collect information about your online activity, even when you use private browsing. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What your internet provider can see when you browse
Your internet service provider, or ISP, acts as the middleman between your devices and the internet. Every website you visit and every online service you use passes through its network.

If you are not using a VPN, your ISP can generally see which websites you are connecting to, when you are online, how much data you are using and your approximate location based on your IP address. Encrypted websites, which begin with "https://," help prevent your provider from reading the contents of most web pages or messages. However, your ISP can still often see that you connected to a certain website in the first place. That information alone can reveal a lot about your interests, routines and habits.
What websites can learn from your visit

Even if you never create an account, some websites can still learn quite a bit about your visit. They can identify your IP address, estimate your location, determine what device and browser you are using and record which pages you viewed.

Some websites also use analytics tools, tracking pixels and advertising scripts to understand how visitors interact with their pages. These tools can show what links you clicked, how long you stayed and which content got your attention.

In some cases, this information may also be shared with advertising or analytics companies. That is one reason you may see ads that seem closely connected to something you recently searched for, viewed or clicked.
ARE APPLE DEVICES SPYING? WHAT YOUR IPHONE TRACKS
Private browsing keeps your history off the device after you close the window, but it does not hide your activity from websites or internet providers. (Neil Godwin/Getty Images)
Why private browsing does not make you invisible
Private browsing tabs, also known as incognito mode in some browsers, can be useful. They help prevent your browser from saving your local browsing history after you close the window.

However, private browsing does not make you invisible online. Websites can still see your visit while you are on their pages. Your internet provider can still see many of the sites you connect to. If you are using a work, school or public network, the network owner may also be able to monitor certain activity.

Private browsing is better thought of as a local privacy tool. It helps hide activity from someone else using the same device later, but it does not fully hide you from websites, advertisers or your internet provider while you are online.
How to reduce what others can see

You cannot eliminate online tracking entirely, but you can make it harder for companies to collect information about you. Start by reviewing your browser's privacy settings. Turn off unnecessary website permissions, such as location, microphone and camera access for sites that do not need them. Consider using a privacy-focused browser or search engine that collects less personal data.

You can also check out these 11 easy ways to protect your online privacy for more ways to limit online tracking. You should also limit how much personal information you share online. The more details you provide across websites, apps and accounts, the easier it becomes for companies to connect your activity. Most importantly, consider using a VPN.
How a VPN helps protect your browsing activity

A VPN, or virtual private network, encrypts your internet traffic before it leaves your device. Instead of your internet provider seeing which websites you are connecting to, it sees an encrypted connection to the VPN server. That makes it much harder for your ISP to build a browsing profile based on your online activity.

A VPN can also help protect your information on public Wi-Fi networks and mask your IP address from websites, advertisers and other third parties. However, a VPN does not stop every type of online tracking. Websites may still recognize you when you log in to an account, use the same browser or share personal details.
A solid VPN makes this process easier by offering apps for computers, smartphones, tablets, smart TVs and routers. That allows you to protect multiple devices with one account.

A VPN can encrypt your internet traffic and mask your IP address, but it cannot stop every form of online tracking. (MANDEL NGAN/AFP via Getty Images)
Quick online privacy checklist
The next time you go online, remember these steps:

Kurt's key takeaways

The internet is built around data, and several companies can collect information every time you browse. Internet providers can see where you are connecting, websites can monitor visits and advertising companies can use tracking tools to build profiles over time. You cannot disappear completely, but you can reduce what others learn about you. A few privacy-minded habits, combined with a trusted VPN, can help you take back more control of your online activity.

title: Your home is empty. Do burglars already know?
summary: Burglary crews linked to Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce break-ins used public schedules and data brokers to target homes while owners traveled.
story: Retired LAPD lieutenant Jeff Wenninger explains how criminals exploit obituaries, routines and public clues to time home break-ins and what families can do to reduce risk.
In Argentina, authorities recently arrested three Chilean men wanted in the U.S. in connection with a South American theft group accused of burglarizing the homes of professional athletes.

Federal prosecutors linked the group to break-ins involving Kansas City Chiefs stars Patrick Mahomes and Travis Kelce, Milwaukee Bucks player Bobby Portis and other athletes. Two of the suspects were also arrested in connection with a burglary at the home of tennis legend Juan Martín del Potro in Argentina.

According to prosecutors, the group identified targets through publicly available schedules and location information, then struck while athletes were away or playing games. Separately, the FBI has warned that international theft groups surveil homeowners to learn their routines and advises travelers to avoid announcing vacations on social media.

Online criminals can research your address, family, travel plans and estimated property value without ever driving down your street. Here's how criminals piece together those digital clues and what you can do to make your home harder to target.
ALLEGED BURGLARY CREW THAT TARGETED PATRICK MAHOMES AND TRAVIS KELCE HOMES ARRESTED IN ARGENTINA: REPORT

Alleged members of a South American theft ring pose with stolen valuables. Federal investigators say the group targeted professional athletes while they were away competing in games. (U.S. Attorney's Office, Middle District of Florida/Photo by Bryan M. Bennett/Getty Images)
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages. You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
How online criminals target empty homes

It may be tempting to assume these crimes only affect people with mansions, expensive cars and celebrity lifestyles. Those cases make the news, but professional athletes and entertainers are far from the only targets. Security researchers and law enforcement agencies have tracked burglary crews using the same methods against everyday homeowners.

One recent case involved a Los Angeles content creator whose Silver Lake home was burglarized while she was traveling. Thieves reportedly took tens of thousands of dollars in designer goods. She had shared that she was away, which gave anyone watching her public account a useful clue.

For retirees, the risk can grow as travel becomes more frequent. You may finally take the cruise you have planned for years, spend a month in Florida each winter or take a road trip to visit your grandchildren. Those trips also create more opportunities to post "we made it" from an airport, beach or campground while your home sits empty.
How family members can expose your travel plans

Maybe you wait until you return home before posting vacation photos. However, someone in your life may share the information for you. A spouse might tag the airport. An adult child could post a picture of the grandchildren in front of your house. A neighbor might mention that you are away on your annual trip.

You have limited control over what other people share, so talk with your family before traveling. Ask everyone to wait until you return before posting locations, travel photos or details about how long you will be gone. Watching what your family posts helps, but social media provides only part of the information criminals can collect.
How property records help criminals research your home

Investigators in Riverside, California, say they routinely find Zillow and Redfin searches on the phones of arrested burglary suspects. These sites may reveal an estimated property value, past sale prices and photos from an old listing. In some cases, criminals can view interior layouts, doors, windows and rooms before they approach the property.

Public property records can also reveal the owner's name, mailing address and purchase history. Meanwhile, data broker and people-search sites may connect that address with phone numbers, relatives, previous homes and other personal details. Combine "this person is traveling" with "this home has significant value," and criminals have the beginnings of a target list.
AI VOICE SCAMS CAN CLONE YOUR FAMILY’S VOICE
Burglars can use social media posts, public records and real estate listings to determine when a home may be empty. (PC Photography / Getty Images)
What strangers can find about your home online

Search your name, phone number and home address to see what appears. You may find people-search profiles that list your age, relatives, address history and possible phone numbers. Real estate websites may still display old interior photos, even when you purchased the home years ago. Someone could use those details to connect your social media account with a specific property.

Want to see what information data brokers may have about you? Run a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web: Cyberguy.com. You should receive the results within an hour.
8 ways to protect your home before your next trip

These steps can reduce the amount of useful information available to someone researching your home. They work best alongside basic home security measures, such as an alarm system, a doorbell camera, light timers and secure storage for valuables.
Save airport, hotel and sightseeing photos until you are back home. Real-time posts can tell strangers where you are and confirm that your house may be empty.
Tell your spouse, children, grandchildren and travel companions to wait before sharing your location or mentioning your travel dates.
Limit posts to people you know. Remove followers you do not recognize and check whether old public posts reveal your routines, vehicles or home address.
Ask a trusted neighbor to collect mail, newspapers and deliveries. You can also place a temporary hold on your mail before an extended trip.
Use timers or smart plugs to turn lights on and off at different times. Leaving every light off for two weeks can make an empty home easier to spot.
WHAT A SCAMMER SEES THE MOMENT THEY GOOGLE YOUR NAME
Surveillance footage shows a 2024 looting carried out by a Chilean crime ring at a Michigan home, shared with Fox 2 Detroit by a homeowner. (WJBK)
Search your address on Zillow, Redfin and other real estate sites to see whether old listings reveal interior rooms, entrances or the layout of your home.

On Redfin, use a desktop browser and sign in. Select your name in the upper-right corner, choose My homes, select your claimed property and click Edit Photos. Check Hide listing photos, then select Yes, Hide Photos. This feature applies to off-market homes and currently does not appear in the Redfin mobile app.

On Zillow, sign in and select your profile icon, followed by Your Home. Choose your property and claim ownership if you have not already done so. From the Owner View, select Edit Facts. You can remove individual photos, delete all photos or check the option to hide photos from public view. Select Save Changes when finished.

Some off-market homes may not offer the editing option. In that case, submit a request to Zillow Customer Support. Other real estate sites may require you to claim the property, contact customer support or ask the original listing agent for help.
Data broker and people-search sites can connect your name, phone number, relatives and home address. Search for your information and request removal from sites that display it.

A data removal service can automate requests across hundreds of covered brokers and continue checking whether your information returns. It cannot erase government property records or every old real estate listing, so use it alongside the other home protection steps above.
You can also submit removal requests yourself, though the process may take more time and require repeat checks.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com.
Search your name, address and phone number every few months. Look for new people-search profiles, outdated listings and social media posts that reveal more than you intended.
Kurt's key takeaways

Burglary crews no longer need to spend days watching your street. Social media can reveal when you are away, while property records, real estate listings and people-search sites can reveal where you live and what your home may be worth. Retirement often brings more time for travel, which creates more opportunities for you or a family member to announce that your home is empty. You have limited control over public records and what your relatives post. However, you can delay travel posts, tighten privacy settings, remove old listing photos and reduce your exposure on data broker sites. Removing your personal information will never make you invisible. It can still make your home harder for online criminals to research and target.

title: What to look for in antivirus software without the jargon
summary: A simple antivirus checklist covers real-time protection, malware and ransomware defense, firewall tools and scam detection without technical jargon.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Shopping for antivirus software can feel harder than it should. Many product pages lead with buzzwords, lab scores and long feature lists. Most of us just want a simple answer: Will this help keep my computer safe without making life harder?

That question gets more important every day. Scammers use fake texts, phishing emails, bogus websites and infected downloads to trick you into giving up your money, passwords or access to your personal files.

The good news? You do not need to understand every technical term to make a smart choice. A strong antivirus program should automatically monitor for threats, help block malware and ransomware, include firewall protection and run quietly in the background.
CyberGuy Live: Missed "Sick of Spam?" Get the replay and checklist

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you step by step through simple ways to reduce robocalls, spam texts, junk email and unwanted messages.
