title: Could this African nation become Trump's next terror target as jihadists close in on power?
summary: Mali's gold and lithium deposits add a minerals dimension as Trump's team reportedly weighs strikes against al Qaeda-linked terrorists in the Sahel.
story: Africa Command Gen. Dagvin Anderson tells lawmakers that shrinking U.S. presence in Africa has weakened intelligence capabilities as Russia, China and terrorist groups expand influence across the continent.
JOHANNESBURG: The U.S. is reportedly considering airstrikes against al Qaeda-linked terrorists in Mali, according to regional analysts and recent media reports.

The military junta that has been running this West African country in the Sahel region since coups in both 2020 and 2021 turned away from France and the U.S. to get military protection from Russia and its Africa Corps mercenaries against jihadist groups.

But now the largest of these groups, Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which has Mali’s capital under siege, is credited, along with another group, for killing 50 Malian soldiers this month, for the death of the country’s defense minister earlier this year and has reportedly sent battalions of Russian soldiers retreating on at least two occasions this year.
ISIS POISED TO EXPLOIT HISTORIC US IRAQ EXIT, TERROR GROUP 'ACTIVELY WAITING IN THE GAPS,' EXPERT WARNS
Malian troops parade during the country's 65th anniversary of the African nation's independence. (Habib Kouyate/Xinhua via Getty Images)

JNIM is said to want to change the country into an Islamist Jihadist state. If they succeed, Mali would be the first country in the world to be run by a jihadist group. The organization was designated officially as a Foreign Terrorist Organization during the first Trump administration in 2018.
Islamic State (ISIS) jihadist groups are also operating freely in Mali, and are linked to terror groups in neighboring Nigeria.

A State Department official didn’t respond to a Washington Post report that the U.S. is considering strikes against JNIM in Mali, but used strong language Thursday when talking to Fox News Digital, leading analysts to suggest the time for talking may be over.

"The United States unequivocally condemns the terrorist activity in Mali," the official said, adding, "in the Sahel, the United States is committed to promoting regional ownership and cooperation against terrorist threats, and monitoring indicators and warnings of threats to our homeland."

This undated photograph handed out by the French military shows three Russian mercenaries, right, in northern Mali. Russia has engaged in under-the-radar military operations in at least half a dozen countries in Africa in the last five years using a shadowy mercenary force analysts say is loyal to President Vladimir Putin. The analysts say the Wagner Group of mercenaries is also key to Putin's ambitions to re-impose Russian influence on a global scale. (French Army via AP)

Edmund Fitton-Brown, a former British and United Nations diplomat, said the U.S. could order military action, to primarily try and stop jihadists becoming entrenched in Mali. Fitton-Brown, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital, "Mali is mainly important to the U.S. because, as a failed state becoming a safe haven for al Qaeda and ISIS, it looks like the first of several African dominoes likely to fall."

Retired U.S. Air Force Maj. Gen. Kenneth P. Ekman, who until last year, served as the Department of War’s West Africa Coordination Element lead, said that with strike action the administration may be able to persuade Mali’s rulers to turn away from Russia, and towards the U.S. for protection – and purchases of military equipment.
RESOURCE-RICH NATION PRAISES US TIES AMID WASHINGTON-BEIJING CRITICAL MINERALS RACE

A column of black smoke rises above buildings as traffic passes the Africa Tower monument in Bamako on April 26, 2026. April 25, 2026's shock attacks, synchronized by Tuareg rebels of the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) coalition and the jihadist Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM), targeted several areas in the vast arid country. Fighting resumed on April 26 in several areas, including Kita near Bamako, Kidal, Gao and Severe.Tuareg rebels meanwhile announced an agreement allowing Russian forces backing Mali's army to withdraw from the northern city of Kidal, which they claimed was "totally" under their control. (AFP via Getty Images)

Ekman told Fox News Digital, "JNIM has a stranglehold on the government and much of the population. The Russians are woefully ineffective and extractive. Cooperation with U.S. forces offers a disproportionate and positive impact."

Ekman said that U.S. forces have supported partner-led operations against JNIM before, as recently as 2022, adding "⁠recent proposals amount to returning to similar cooperation against a mutual threat."

The administration may also be in a minerals frame of mind. Mali is one of Africa’s largest gold-producing nations. It also has substantial deposits of lithium, used extensively in rechargeable batteries.
Fitton-Brown said that "President Trump may be less reluctant than his predecessor to work with the juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger, if they are losing faith in their Russian friends."
A vehicle turned up following a brutal ambush on Russian Wagner fighters in Mali on July 27, 2024. (East2West)

He continued, "The U.S. is certainly a more capable partner. France has already been displaced, so all three countries might accept U.S. help if it comes only with strings attached that don’t offend or disadvantage them. Whether even the U.S. is capable of stopping the political decline of these countries, and the rise of militant Islam, is another matter. That cannot be achieved by military force alone."

The FDD’s Fitton-Brown said U.S. assets such as aircraft may not be directly involved if there is a strike, "The U.S. might work with French and other intelligence services to develop local intelligence for strikes on JNIM leadership, but this is unlikely to achieve much. The organization is resilient and will be able to replace those killed."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A former senior Department of War official told Fox News Digital the U.S. has at its disposal cruise missiles and long-range bombers. Attack drones would probably not come into play, and the U.S. Naval Institute’s Fleet Tracker shows no American aircraft carriers anywhere near African waters, effectively ruling out carrier operations.
However, Ekman believes airstrikes are under consideration, noting "JNIM and ISIS are a threat to U.S. interests, and are ascendant in West Africa."
Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Is Israel really isolated? Polls and diplomacy point in opposite directions
summary: Trump says the Saudi Arabia nuclear deal hinges on joining the Abraham Accords, as experts debate whether Israel faces isolation or expanding ties.
story: Richard Goldberg argues that Israel’s strategic relationships are expanding even as opposition grows among Democrats, international institutions and parts of Western public opinion.

President Donald Trump predicted in recent days that additional countries would soon join the Abraham Accords, renewing debate over whether Israel is becoming increasingly isolated or continuing to expand its most important strategic relationships.

"The Abraham Accords have been, I think, a tremendous success," Trump said during a Tuesday Oval Office meeting with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun. "I think you’re going to see a lot of countries joining pretty soon."

Trump's prediction underscores a central debate about Israel's global position: Public support for the country has fallen sharply in the United States and across much of the world, yet Israel continues to build or preserve diplomatic, military, energy and technology relationships with foreign governments.
TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS
President Donald Trump predicted in recent days that additional countries would soon join the Abraham Accords. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

The Abraham Accords, brokered by the Trump administration in 2020, normalized relations between Israel and the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan. Trump has made expanding the agreements a central goal of his Middle East strategy.

The dispute depends partly on how isolation is measured. Critics point to worsening public opinion, pressure at international institutions and growing opposition among Democrats and younger voters. Israeli officials and conservative foreign-policy experts argue that government-to-government cooperation remains strong and, in some regions, is expanding.

Trump reinforced that strategy Thursday by saying a U.S. civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia would depend on the kingdom joining the Abraham Accords. The statement showed the administration attempting to use one of Washington’s most valuable offers to Riyadh to secure normalization with Israel, but it did not demonstrate that Saudi Arabia had agreed to do so.
Israeli Ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon rejected the contention that Israel had become isolated.

"The claim that Israel is an isolated country is simply not true," Danon told Fox News Digital. "While the campaign to dismantle the Hamas terrorist organization has drawn international criticism, Israel’s relationships with other countries have not weakened. They have evolved."

Former White House national security official Richard Goldberg similarly argued that Israel retains strong support among conservatives and that its electoral gains are translating into closer government relations.

"Polling in the United States shows massive support among conservatives and Republicans, including self-described MAGA, for Israel still," Goldberg told Fox News Digital. "And that’s reflected around the world, particularly among conservative candidates and parties that win elected office right now."

Goldberg pointed to political changes in Latin America, expanding partnerships in the Eastern Mediterranean and Israel’s continuing defense and technology relationships as evidence that public criticism has not translated into comprehensive strategic isolation.
The dispute comes amid polling that shows Israel retaining deep support among Republicans while losing ground across the broader American electorate and much of the world.
POTENTIAL 2028 DEM CONTENDER UNLOADS ON NETANYAHU, ADMITS US-ISRAEL TIES AT 'CROSSROADS'
Anti-Israel protests in Istanbul. (Bulent Kilic/AFP via Getty Images)

Eighty percent of self-identified MAGA Republicans said Israel’s security matters to U.S. security and prosperity, a Reagan Institute survey released in June found, while 73% supported sending Israel U.S. weapons. Among MAGA Republicans under 30, 63% said Israel’s security matters to the United States and 60% supported sending weapons.

The same survey found that broader support was narrowing. Sixty-five percent of Americans said Israel’s security matters to U.S. security and prosperity, down six percentage points from a year earlier.
The figure fell nine points among Democrats to 57%, compared with 75% of Republicans and 80% of MAGA Republicans.

A Pew Research Center survey published in June found that a median of 67% of adults across 36 countries viewed Israel unfavorably, while 25% viewed it favorably. The findings came from Pew’s Spring 2026 Global Attitudes Survey.

In the United States, 60% of adults viewed Israel unfavorably, up from 53% in 2025 and 42% in 2022, according to a separate Pew survey conducted March 23 to March 29. Eighty percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents held an unfavorable view, while negative assessments were also widespread among adults under 50.

Israel no longer held a statistically significant advantage over the Palestinians in Americans’ sympathies, Gallup reported in February. Forty-one percent said they sympathized more with the Palestinians and 36% with the Israelis, although Gallup said the five-point difference was not statistically significant.
In 2023, 54% sympathized more with Israelis and 31% with Palestinians.
Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel highlighted that erosion during a July 8 speech at Tel Aviv University.
"Support for Israel around the world is declining," Emanuel said, "The only diplomatic achievement Israel has secured in the past three years is Somaliland."
THE US-ISRAEL STRATEGIC ALLIANCE – PARTNERSHIP, NOT CHARITY
Anti-Israel activists hold banners that include, "globalize the intifada" during a protest commemorating Nakba Day May 15, 2025, in Brooklyn, New York. (Alexi Rosenfeld/Getty Images)

Emanuel’s conclusion focuses on Israel’s declining public legitimacy and its strained position in traditional diplomatic institutions. Goldberg and Danon argue that it overlooks expanding government-to-government relationships built around defense, intelligence, energy, technology and trade.
Goldberg pointed in particular to Latin America, where he said newly elected conservative governments have made closer ties with Israel an early priority.

"Every time a government in South America right now flips from left wing to right wing, one of the first things they do is reestablish better relations with Israel, withdraw recognition of a Palestinian state and see what else they can do to make Israel a strategic partner," Goldberg said.
He cited Argentina under President Javier Milei and the proposed "Isaac Accords," along with political changes in Chile, Colombia and Bolivia, as evidence of a broader realignment.
Goldberg also argued that Israel remains central to emerging partnerships involving energy, defense, intelligence and critical infrastructure.

"If you’re in the Eastern Mediterranean and you’re Greece and you are Cyprus, you’re thinking about how do we work with Israel to make the Eastern Mediterranean partnership even stronger," he said. "If you’re Armenia and Azerbaijan in a tough neighborhood between Turkey and Iran, you’re talking to Israel, you’re getting closer to Israel."

Israel, Greece and Cyprus reaffirmed their strategic partnership during a trilateral summit in December 2025, agreeing to expand cooperation in energy, security, emergency preparedness and regional connectivity.
Danon said the diplomatic shift is visible even inside the United Nations, an institution where Israel routinely faces critical resolutions and public condemnation.

"We see this every day in the corridors of the United Nations," he said. "While many South American countries were once highly critical of Israel in recent years, we are now cooperating with many of them. These discussions are happening in public and behind the scenes."

"As Israel’s official representative to the United Nations, I regularly meet with ambassadors from around the world, including from Arab countries, to quietly advance initiatives where we share common interests," Danon said.
Danon went further than Goldberg in assessing Israel’s position since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attacks and the subsequent war.

"Compared to the period before October 7, Israel is in a far stronger geostrategic position," Danon said. "That is reflected not only in regional developments but also in the country’s diplomatic relationships around the world."
The competing evidence suggests that much of the disagreement depends on how isolation is defined.

Israel may be losing public support and influence in traditional international institutions while simultaneously preserving or expanding government-to-government cooperation in defense, technology, intelligence, energy and agriculture.
MAMDANI GOES BACK ON CAMPAIGN PROMISE, SAYS NYC CAN’T ARREST NETANYAHU

European Union Council President, Charles Michel (center), Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (right) and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu (left) meet in January 2020 in West Jerusalem. (PhKobi Gideon / GPO / Handout/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)
Goldberg acknowledged that relationships driven by conservative political victories could become vulnerable when governments change.
But he argued that Israel is increasingly building relationships around durable national interests rather than political ideology alone.

The central risk for Israel is that today’s collapse in public opinion could eventually reshape tomorrow’s government policies. Conservative governments may currently protect and expand strategic ties, but younger voters and left-wing parties could alter those relationships after future elections.
Israel is scheduled to hold national elections Oct. 27, the country’s first since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks.
Goldberg argued that a change in Israel’s government would provide a test of whether international opposition is directed primarily at Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or at Israel itself.

"If there is somebody else who becomes prime minister next, we will have to evaluate," Goldberg said. "Those very loud detractors of Israel who right now use Netanyahu as their symbol for bashing and say it’s not about Israel, it’s about Netanyahu, they’ll be put to the test very quickly."
He noted that the boycott movement and anti-Israel campus organizations remained active during the previous government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, when Netanyahu was not prime minister.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

President Donald Trump predicted in recent days that additional countries would soon join the Abraham Accords, renewing debate over whether Israel is becoming increasingly isolated or continuing to expand its most important strategic relationships. (Dan Kitwood/Getty Images)
"Is their hatred and venom really just about Bibi Netanyahu, or is it fundamentally about a Jewish state that they don’t like existing?" Goldberg asked.

For now, both realities appear to be unfolding at once: Israel remains a sought-after military, intelligence and technology partner for a growing group of governments, while its support among the global public has fallen to levels that could eventually threaten those relationships.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is an investigative journalist, filmmaker and war correspondent. She has directed and produced over 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries. Recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award, Lachter is also a 2023-24 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: French modeling scout linked to Jeffrey Epstein found dead in Paris apartment
summary: Daniel Siad's name appeared roughly 2,000 times in the Epstein files, and at least 24 women came forward as alleged victims or witnesses in a trafficking probe.
story: Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche pushed back July 15, 2026, on claims the DOJ has closed the book on Jeffrey Epstein's crimes, saying prosecutors are ready to pursue anyone criminally linked to the late financier's trafficking operation.
A French modeling scout with ties to Jeffrey Epstein was found dead inside his Paris apartment, prosecutors said.
The body of Daniel Siad, 69, was discovered Monday night, and an autopsy is pending. Siad's attorney, Menya Arab-Tigrine, told Fox News Digital he died of a heart attack.

"While he died of a heart attack, the unbearable waiting, the stigma cast upon him and, by extension, his loved ones as well as the daily pressure and anxiety he endured, undoubtedly played a role," she said. "We must await the autopsy results to determine whether his body simply gave out."
Fox News Digital has reached out to French prosecutors.
JEFFREY EPSTEIN'S PURPORTED SUICIDE NOTE UNSEALED BY FEDERAL JUDGE IN CELLMATE'S CASE
Daniel Siad, 69, a French modeling scout with ties to Jeffrey Epstein, was found dead inside his Paris apartment, prosecutors said Wednesday. (Justice Department)
Siad's name appeared about 2,000 times in the Epstein files released by the Justice Department, Reuters reported.
"I am here in Barcelona I have girls staying with me from Australia Croecian origin, so you can speak with her very Sweet," Siad allegedly wrote to Epstein in one email.
"I am looking to place her here and Paris."
DEMOCRAT CALLS HOWARD LUTNICK A 'PATHOLOGICAL LIAR' AFTER CLOSED-DOOR EPSTEIN TESTIMONY

This photograph taken July 22, 2026, shows the home of model agent Daniel Siad in Colombes, a north-western suburb of Paris, where he was found dead July 20. Authorities opened an investigation into the cause of death and ordered a postmortem examination. (AFP via Getty Images)
"Photo?" Epstein replied.
Another email from Siad to Epstein from April 2009 included images of a 17-year-old Slovakian girl while he was scouting models in Bratislava.

At least 24 women have come forward as victims or witnesses of alleged acts committed by Siad or others after the February launch of a human trafficking and fraud probe, Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau told Reuters.
Jeffrey Epstein was found dead in federal custody in 2019. (New York State Sex Offender Registry via AP, File)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Investigators looked into Siad, but there wasn't enough evidence to justify his immediate arrest, said Arab-Tigrine.

"Let us not forget that he was never prosecuted, nor was he ever formally implicated in any legal proceedings," she said. "In the coming days, we must respect the grief of his loved ones. He has passed away, and he was innocent."
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Nicaragua's parliament plans to eliminate elections to codify President Ortega's declaration
summary: Nicaragua's congress moves to abolish elections after President Daniel Ortega declared no more elections, drawing condemnation from the international community.
story: Sen. Ron Johnson responds to New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill's admission of 6,600 non-citizens improperly registered to vote due to a software error, with 400 actually voting. Johnson, from Wisconsin, stresses that election integrity, including voter ID and cleaning voter rolls, should be a non-partisan issue to restore public confidence in U.S. elections.

Nicaragua's lawmakers announced plans to abolish elections in the Central American country, following through on President Daniel Ortega's declaration over the weekend that there would be no more elections, which enraged the international community.

The move was revealed on Tuesday by Nicaragua's congress, which is firmly in the hands of Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo. Lawmakers said the planned constitutional overhaul will ensure Nicaragua's "peace, security and stability."

With the announcement, lawmakers are making good on Ortega's promise of no more elections, further closing off any potential path for the opposition to challenge the government he leads with Murillo, whom constitutional reforms elevated from vice president to "co-president."

"There won't be any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and seize power," Ortega said on Sunday during a speech commemorating the 1979 Sandinista revolution, in which Ortega participated in the overthrow of the U.S.-backed dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza.
NICARAGUA'S ORTEGA SAYS COUNTRY WILL 'NEVER AGAIN' HOLD ELECTIONS, SHUTTING OUT OPPOSITION
Nicaragua's President Daniel Ortega said officials in the Central American country will no longer hold elections. (Reuters/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria)
"The days when parties backed by the Yankees (United States) and the Somocistas would return to power are over — never again," he declared.
The declaration appeared to eliminate the possibility of a future electoral challenge as Ortega and Murillo continue consolidating control over the country’s political institutions.

Ortega and Murillo expanded their authority through sweeping constitutional changes that took effect in 2025. The reforms included extending the presidential term from five years to six and placing the legislative, judicial and electoral institutions under the authority of the presidency.
The pair now exercise control over nearly every branch of government, including the armed forces, police and judiciary.

Ortega, Nicaragua’s longest-serving leader, is scheduled to remain in office until early 2028, although his statement on Sunday effectively canceled Nicaragua’s next elections, which had been scheduled for November 2027.
Critics say Ortega had already effectively eliminated meaningful electoral competition during elections in 2011, 2016 and 2021.
REPUBLICAN REP MARÍA ELVIRA SALAZAR DECLARES, 'AFTER CUBA, NICARAGUA IS NEXT'
President Daniel Ortega's promise to abolish elections prompted widespread condemnation from the international community. (Carlos Becerra/Bloomberg)

Many prominent opposition leaders have been imprisoned, forced into exile or stripped of their Nicaraguan citizenship, while opposition parties and independent civic organizations have lost their legal status.

A United Nations group of experts has accused the Ortega-Murillo government of systematically violating human rights as part of a campaign to eliminate criticism and preserve its hold on power. The experts said some alleged violations may amount to crimes against humanity.
The government launched a violent crackdown on anti-government protests in 2018. More than 300 people were killed during the unrest, according to international human rights groups.
Ortega's effort to abolish elections prompted widespread condemnation from foreign governments, including the U.S.

"Daniel Ortega’s declaration that, under his family’s dictatorship, Nicaragua will never again hold elections lays bare their true authoritarian nature. Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo have abandoned even the pretense of popular consent," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday.

"The Nicaraguan people have the right to choose their own leaders through democratic elections. The United States calls on the international community to join forces to demonstrate to the Murillo-Ortega dictatorship that it cannot expect to maintain business as usual with other nations when it is thwarting the basic tenets of our democratic hemisphere," he added.
The move to abolish elections was announced by Nicaragua's congress, which is firmly in the hands of President Daniel Ortega and his wife, Rosario Murillo. (INTI OCON/AFP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Trump administration has described the Ortega-Murillo government as a dictatorship and imposed sanctions on members of the government and their allies. The State Department has also enacted visa restrictions targeting more than 2,350 Nicaraguan officials and their family members.

Volker Türk, the United Nations' high commissioner for human rights, denounced Nicaragua's legislative ambitions on Wednesday, saying that "people of all political viewpoints must be allowed to vote and run for office."
"These latest developments further deepen the severe restrictions on fundamental freedoms, the dismantling of civic space, and the steady erosion of the rule of law," Türk said in a statement.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

title: Israeli UN envoy blasts Mamdani as 'clown' over call to arrest Netanyahu: 'It's a stunt'
summary: Israel's UN ambassador called Mayor Zohran Mamdani a "clown" after he demanded federal authorities arrest Benjamin Netanyahu on an ICC warrant.
story: Thiessen criticizes Mamdani for calling on federal authorities to arrest Netanyahu on an International Criminal Court warrant despite a lack of legal authority.

Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations on Wednesday blasted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as a "clown" for demanding federal authorities arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu when Netanyahu arrives in the city.

Danny Danon’s remarks came after Mamdani accused Netanyahu of being a "war criminal" and the "architect of a horrific genocide" against Palestinians while calling on the federal government to execute an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against the Israeli leader.
Netanyahu is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in Manhattan in September.
NETANYAHU FIRES BACK AT NYC MAYOR MAMDANI'S VOW TO ENFORCE 'BOGUS ARREST WARRANT'

Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon speaks during a United Nations emergency security council meeting on Lebanon at the U.N. Headquarters in New York, on Mar. 31. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)
"Those baseless remarks about harassing the prime minister — it's a joke, and he's a clown," Danon told Fox News Digital Wednesday.

"Everyone knows it's a show. It's a stunt," Danon added. "A mayor should be dealing with the homeless people, the garbage in New York, and leave foreign affairs to the people in Washington who are elected to do it. He should take care of the security of the people in New York, especially the Jewish community, which is seeing the rise of antisemitism. That is his first responsibility."
The YouTube channel for the New York City Mayor's Office released a video July 21, "Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal."
"Benjamin Netanyahu is a war criminal, the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people," Mamdani said, repeating comments he made in an interview with The New York Times.

Mamdani leveled a series of allegations against the Israeli leader, claiming he was "responsible for the killing of more than 73,000 people, for the maiming of tens of thousands of children, as those who survive undergo amputation without anesthesia."
He also accused Netanyahu of targeting neonatal hospitals and maternity care centers and alleged that he blocked food and humanitarian aid.
CNN LEGAL ANALYST CALLS OUT 'UTTERLY RIDICULOUS' CLAIM BY MAMDANI ABOUT NETANYAHU ARREST
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks to reporters during a news conference in New York on Feb. 17, 2026.  (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

"Just last month, the U.N. confirmed that Palestinian children continue to be deliberately targeted and killed by Israeli armed forces, more than eight months after the so-called ceasefire," Mamdani said.
"All as we, as Americans, pay for the bombs that do the killing. There is a reason the International Criminal Court issued a warrant for his arrest."
Danon pushed back sharply against the mayor's accusations.
"There is a lot of humanitarian aid coming into Gaza every day," Danon argued.

"Nobody speaks about those issues anymore, but he wants to resume spreading blood libels, promoting the claims of genocide, starvation and all those lies that were spread by him, by his wife and by other people during the war.
"He wants to go back to this situation, but today there are no humanitarian issues in Gaza," Danon added.
"Mamdani continues to promote those blood libels against Israel and against the Jews."
Mamdani also said that City Hall cannot act on the warrant unilaterally.

"It is clear that we do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant. The federal government, however, does, and I call on them to join the ICC and execute this warrant," Mamdani said.
"Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large."
MAMDANI’S ‘DERANGED’ ISRAEL TAKE RESURFACES AS HE TARGETS NETANYAHU

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said his administration is exploring whether the city has legal authority to arrest Netanyahu, pictured here, if he visits for the U.N. General Assembly. (Ronen Zvulun/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Israeli officials strongly deny all charges. Netanyahu’s office has rejected the ICC’s jurisdiction, labeling it "a kangaroo court that has no jurisdiction over Americans or Israelis."

"People are smart; they know there's no legal basis for his remarks," Danon said. "The U.S. is not part of the ICC. There is no warrant that is actually effective against the prime minister in the U.S. So it's a political stunt."
"We have serious issues to deal with — the war with Iran and other critical matters.
"The prime minister is not actually dealing with Mamdani's remarks at all. He said it very clearly: He intends to come and speak at the U.N.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Prime Minister Netanyahu will come to New York and will speak in the General Assembly," Danon said. "The only thing the mayor can do is come to the U.N., grab a seat, listen to the Prime Minister and maybe learn something from his speech.
"Last year, Mayor Adams came to the prime minister's speech," Danon noted. "A local leader can come and hear. That's the only thing he can do."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: France records more than 5,700 excess deaths during historic early summer heat wave
summary: More than 5,700 excess deaths were recorded during France's unprecedented June heat wave, making it the country's deadliest since 2003, health officials said.
story: Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin discusses the heat wave hitting the U.S. and views on climate change on 'America Reports.'

France has recorded more than 5,700 excess deaths during its historic summer heat wave, marking the country's deadliest heat-related toll in more than two decades, Public Health France announced Wednesday.
Between June 17 and July 2, the agency expected 15,910 deaths but instead recorded 21,674. The difference — 5,764 excess deaths — was 36% higher than what would have been expected.
During the heat wave, temperatures climbed well above 104 degrees Fahrenheit in many parts of the country, Public Health France said.

"This unprecedented event, characterized by its early onset, intensity and duration, exposed almost the entire population to extreme heat during a period that was still largely dedicated to school and work activities," the agency said.
EUROPE'S FIRES REVEAL DEADLY MIX OF RECORD HEAT, HUMAN ERROR, ARSON AND LAND MISMANAGEMENT
Tourists enjoy cooling off at a public water fountain in Paris, Friday, June 26, 2026. (Christophe Ena)
Deaths from all causes increased across hospitals, private homes and nursing homes during the heat wave.

The agency's analysis included people ages 15 and older, with mortality increasing beginning at age 45. Adults 75 and older accounted for roughly two-thirds of the provisional death toll, representing at least 3,719 excess deaths.
SCIENTIST CALLS FOR AMERICANS TO CUT OFF AIR CONDITIONING IN SUMMER, CLAIMING IT CAUSES GLOBAL WARMING
The Paris region was hit hardest, recording 1,999 excess deaths, more than 80% above what would have been expected without the heat wave, according to the agency.

Public Health France said 2026 recorded the country's highest excess mortality linked to a heat wave since 2003. The National Institute of Health and Medical Research estimated that roughly 15,000 more people died compared to the usual mortality for that time of year.
Tourists cool off at a public water fountain in Paris, Friday, June 26, 2026. (Christophe Ena)
PARIS DEPUTY MAYOR BLAMES UNITED STATES' CARBON EMISSIONS FOR DEADLY HEAT WAVE
This year, the hottest days occurred on June 24 and June 25, when the national average temperature reached 86 degrees Fahrenheit. Peak temperatures also climbed above 104 degrees in many areas.
More than half of the excess deaths — about 56% — occurred during or immediately after the most intense stretch of the heat wave between June 25 and June 27.
Officials also said more than 10,000 excess deaths were reported across Europe during the peak of the heat wave, though the preliminary figures are expected to be updated in the coming weeks.
People cool off in a fountain in Paris during a major heat wave. (Abdul Saboor/Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

According to The Associated Press, funeral directors in Paris said they were inundated by the surge in bodies awaiting burial or cremation, with some mortuaries reaching capacity and turning down new arrivals.

Health officials noted that the excess mortality estimate includes deaths from all causes that occurred during the heat wave. The figures remain provisional and will continue to be refined in the coming weeks.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Italy shuts down effort linked to Gaza flotilla group to track Jewish, Israeli tourists
summary: An anonymous online form asked the public to report locations of Israeli tourists and Italian Jews, drawing comparisons to fascist-era persecution.
story: As Vice President JD Vance warns that expanding economic opportunity is key to preventing socialism's rise, Domenech discusses the cultural, political and educational trends he believes are reshaping younger Americans' views on capitalism and the future of the country.

Italian authorities shut down an anonymous online effort that asked the public to report the locations of Israeli tourists, Italian Jews and businesses believed to have ties to Zionism, drawing condemnation from senior government officials and Jewish leaders who compared the initiative to fascist-era persecution.

"I think we’re going back to the 1930s, to hunting Jews," Walker Meghnagi, president of the Jewish Community of Milan, said after the Google form began circulating on social media and messaging platforms.

The questionnaire said it was intended to "map Zionist tourism," property purchases and what it described as "Zionist neo-colonization" in Italy, according to reports. It asked users to identify Jews, Israelis and people believed to be connected to Zionism at hotels, vacation rentals, businesses and other public places.
ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS

People take part in a flash mob entitled "In the same boat" to protest the detention and treatment of activists participating in the Global Sumud Flotilla in Milan, northern Italy, on May 21, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

"The online mapping of so-called 'Zionist tourism,' rightly denounced by the president of the Jewish Community of Milan, Walker Meghnagi, is an aberrant initiative, in direct violation of fundamental human rights and the constitutional principles on which our nation is founded," Italian Senate President Ignazio La Russa wrote in a statement, as translated to English.

"No form of cataloguing of persons on the basis of their religious belief or their connection with Israel is acceptable or justifiable. Behind all this lies a profound anti-Semitism that must be unanimously, firmly, and determinedly rejected," he added. "We cannot remain motionless in the face of such serious facts that recall the ghosts of the past. To the Jewish Community all my closeness."
The form was removed following the intervention of Gen. Pasquale Angelosanto, Italy’s national coordinator for the fight against antisemitism, according to Italian and Israeli media reports.
'NOT ON OUR WATCH': GLOBAL LAW ENFORCEMENT LEADERS UNITE IN POLAND AGAINST HATE

A view of participants in a May 21 flash mob demonstration in Milan, northern Italy, with people gathered in public space to show solidarity with detained Global Sumud Flotilla activists. (AFP via Getty Images)
"This form is intended to record cases of Zionist tourism, property purchases, and, more generally, Zionist neo-colonization in Italy," the questionnaire stated.

It said the information collected would be received by the Global Sumud Movement, an activist network associated with flotilla efforts to reach the Gaza Strip, and would remain confidential. Respondents were asked to provide sources so the reports could be verified and used to coordinate unspecified "initiatives."
The Global Sumud Movement denied commissioning the form or knowing about it before the controversy erupted, according to The Jerusalem Post.

"Zionism is one of the issues we work on, but we do not hunt Jews, and we know nothing about this questionnaire," the group told the Italian newspaper La Repubblica. "We did not commission it and had not even seen it before it was taken offline."
EXILED MUSLIM SCHOLAR WARNS FAR-LEFT–ISLAMIST ALLIANCE BEHIND ANTI-ISRAEL PROTESTS ECHOES IRAN’S RISE

Seen Oct. 2, 2025, in Piazzale Loreto in Milan, Italy, demonstrators participate in a protest supporting the Global Sumud Flotilla after its interception by the Israeli army off the Gaza coast. (Alessandro Bremec/NurPhoto)
The organization said it learned about the questionnaire through news reports and reserved the right to take further action, including issuing a formal statement.

According to La Repubblica, later sections of the form asked respondents to name locations where Jewish or Israeli visitors had been seen and to indicate whether local organizations or activist groups were already "managing the phenomenon."
Meghnagi warned that collecting and circulating such information could encourage extremists to target Jews and Israelis.

"What is happening today shows that there are unbalanced individuals out there, and if this kind of message spreads widely enough, you are certain to find someone willing to act on it," he said. "For this reason, mapping where Jews are is extremely serious."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Alessandro Morelli, an Italian deputy secretary of state, ripped the form as "abhorrent" and said those responsible should not go unpunished.

Eric Mack is a breaking news reporter and writer Sunday through Thursday, 6 a.m. ET to 2 p.m. ET, with a particular interest in stories that lead the news cycle on politics, elections, foreign affairs and government.

title: Rubio accuses Iran of flying IRGC personnel into Yemen as Houthi threat escalates
summary: Marco Rubio accuses Iran of flying IRGC members into Yemen, saying the flights helped ignite a renewed confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis.
story: Dagen McDowell highlights how Iran's financial support of terror proxies, including the Houthis in Yemen, has led to a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia. This significant escalation in the Middle East jeopardizes critical oil shipping lanes in the Red Sea, causing global investors to remain on high alert due to potential economic repercussions.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio accused Iran on Wednesday of flying members of its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps into Yemen, saying Tehran’s actions helped ignite a renewed confrontation between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
"They decided to send direct flights from Tehran into Yemen, carrying IRGC elements and others into the country," Rubio told reporters. "And the Saudis responded to it."
Rubio did not identify the flights, specify how many IRGC personnel were allegedly transported or provide evidence supporting the allegation.
RUBIO SAYS US REMAINS OPEN TO IRAN TALKS BUT WARNS THERE 'WILL BE CONSEQUENCES'

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks during a press conference on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Pasay, Metro Manila on July 22, 2026. (Brendan SMIALOWSKI / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

He made the remarks while attending an annual gathering of Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers in Manila, Philippines, where the U.S.-Iran conflict and threats to international shipping were among the central security concerns.
The Houthis have declared a blockade targeting Saudi-linked vessels in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, threatening to widen the conflict and disrupt another critical global trade route.

The rebels say they are targeting ships connected to Saudi Arabia or traveling to and from the kingdom’s Red Sea ports in retaliation for Saudi restrictions on Yemen and a recent attack on the airport in the Houthi-controlled capital of Sanaa.
IRAN-BACKED TERROR PROXY HOUTHIS THREATEN FRESH ATTACKS AFTER YEMEN AIRPORT STRIKE
Oil tankers and cargo ships line up in the Strait of Hormuz as seen from Khor Fakkan, United Arab Emirates, Wednesday, March 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Altaf Qadri)

The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the airport attack, which they said was intended to stop a flight carrying Houthi leaders home from Iran. Rubio disputed that account and alleged that Tehran was using direct flights to transport IRGC personnel and others into Yemen.
The Houthis later launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia’s Abha International Airport, marking one of the most serious confrontations between the two sides in years.
Rubio said U.S. officials had spoken repeatedly with Saudi officials during the past week about the Houthi threat.
IRAN CALLS ON HOUTHIS TO PREPARE TO CUT OFF RED SEA GATEWAY — CAN THE TERROR GROUP DO IT?
"Anything that restricts shipping through the Red Sea would be problematic for the same reasons that the Strait of Hormuz is problematic," Rubio said. "So we’re watching that closely."
Saudi Arabia’s military has vowed to keep Bab el-Mandeb open and respond firmly to Houthi threats against commercial vessels using the waterway.

The narrow strait connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and serves as a major shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal. Around 12% of global trade and roughly one-quarter of worldwide container traffic normally pass through the route.

Its importance has grown as the U.S.-Iran conflict has sharply curtailed shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi Arabia has increasingly relied on Red Sea export routes to transport oil to international markets.
A Houthi follower looks on, during a pro-Iran demonstration, as the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran continues, in Sanaa, Yemen April 6, 2026. (Khaled Abdullah/Reuters)
The Houthi-run SABA news agency claimed six vessels had altered course after receiving warnings from the group, a claim that could not be independently verified.

The Houthis say the blockade is limited to Saudi-linked shipping. During their earlier campaign connected to the war in Gaza, however, the rebels attacked more than 100 vessels, including ships with little or no apparent connection to Israel.
President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the latest Houthi threat had not materialized.
"So far, it hasn’t happened," Trump told reporters. "I think that if there is something like that, we’ll just have to take care of business."

Rubio’s accusation came as the U.S. military carried out an 11th consecutive night of strikes against targets in Iran. U.S. Central Command said the latest targets included aircraft hangars and drone storage sites.

Speaking to Southeast Asian leaders, Rubio also warned that allowing Iran to control the Strait of Hormuz, collect tolls and attack ships that refused to comply would set a dangerous precedent for international waterways around the world.

"If we create a precedent in the Middle East where a nation state can decide that they are going to control an international waterway, charge a toll and, if you don’t pay them, blow up your ships, we have created a very dangerous precedent which will repeat itself in other parts of the world, including in this region," Rubio said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rubio said Iran’s support for the Houthis reflects a broader pattern of backing armed groups across the Middle East.

"The Houthis, Hezbollah, the militias in Iraq, Hamas — this is what Iran spends its money on," Rubio said. "It’s not on its people. It’s on supporting terrorist organizations and destabilizing actors in the region."
Bradford Betz is a Fox News Digital breaking reporter covering crime, political issues, and much more.

title: Washington says goodbye to Sen. Lindsey Graham
summary: A special ceremony at the Capitol and a funeral service at the National Cathedral on Tuesday will be private, but both events will be livestreamed for the public.
story: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump, congressional colleagues and world leaders Tuesday will say their final goodbyes to Sen. Lindsey Graham, the influential and colorful foreign policy hawk whose sudden death this month at age 71 stunned Washington and reverberated in capitals around the globe.

Two days of ceremonies and funeral services began Tuesday morning when Graham’s American flag-draped casket arrived at the Capitol for a special ceremony in the rotunda — his last visit to a building where he served for more than three decades.

In honor of the senator’s long military career, an armed forces body bearer team slowly carried his casket up the Capitol steps. Graham served as an Air Force judge advocate general, or JAG, officer and retired from the Air Force Reserve in 2015 with the rank of colonel.

Senate colleagues, past and present, Cabinet members and Graham’s family and staffers packed the Rotunda. Among those paying tribute were former Sens. Bob Corker and Lamar Alexander, both Tennessee Republicans; Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Richard Burr, R-N.C.; Jeff Flake, R-Ariz.; Pat Toomey, R-Pa.; and Kelly Ayotte, now New Hampshire’s GOP governor.

“It’s such a loss in terms of his voice on foreign policy and America’s role in the world,” Ayotte, who traveled regularly with Graham on Senate trips around the world, told NBC News, adding: “He loved life, he had so much fun, and no one could make you laugh more than Lindsey Graham.”
Vice President JD Vance, who also served with Graham in the Senate, remembered the late senator’s “swashbuckling, infectious laugh” and called him a “true American original.”

Graham, Vance said, had a common touch, likely from his humble upbringing in western South Carolina, and could connect with all people, whether it was political leaders or the waitstaff in the Capitol.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

“Lindsey Graham loved people from all walks of life. … He was fascinated in the waitstaff in the Senate dining room. He was fascinated in the people who made the food. He was fascinated in the lowest staffer who had been hired three days earlier,” Vance said at the Capitol ceremony. “He was fascinated by, of course, the very leadership of our country, and I think he was fascinated in people because he loved people.”

Others on hand were former South Carolina Rep. Trey Gowdy, a Fox News host; acting Attorney General Todd Blanche; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former senator; and White House budget director Russell Vought.

“It’s difficult to believe that we’re here today to say a final farewell to Lindsey as he leaves the Capitol for the last time. My heart is heavy,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said at the ceremony.

“Lindsey was a towering figure here in the Senate and on the international stage. ... Lindsey will be remembered as a senator and as a statesman,” Thune said. “But for me, most of all, I will remember him as my friend. It’s hard to think that there will be no more Senate dinners with Lindsey.”

Graham’s sister and only sibling, Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace him in the Senate, walked tearfully up to the casket alone, then placed her hand on the casket. Backed by Trump, she is running for a full term in an Aug. 11 primary.
She was joined by her family. Then a parade of Trump officials, senators and Senate staffers paid tribute. Former Sen. Burr kissed the casket “to say goodbye.”
“He was one of our close friends,” Burr said.
From the Capitol, Graham’s casket departed for the Washington National Cathedral for an invitation-only funeral service at 2 p.m. ET. That will be livestreamed.

Trump is expected to speak at the funeral. Cabinet officials and congressional and military leaders are expected to be on hand, as are global leaders who viewed Graham as a key American ally on defense and foreign policy matters, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Graham didn’t come close to winning the presidency when he ran against Trump in 2016, but Tuesday’s send-off in the nation’s capital was fit for a president, with Trump, Vance and world leaders personally honoring Graham.
Graham did not lie in state or honor in the Capitol rotunda, but few other lawmakers have received such a ceremony.

It was a testament to Graham’s political influence and longevity. In addition to his 33-year military career, Graham had previously served as Senate Judiciary Committee chairman and was Budget Committee chairman when he died. He was also one of the most quoted members of Congress; he was a regular on Fox News and had logged 63 appearances on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“He’s been one of a kind, irreplaceable. dedicated his life to this country. I mean, in the end, gave his life to this country. I mean, all the arduous travel took a toll on him,” said Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who succeeded Graham as Budget chairman upon his death.
“Nobody had a quicker wit ... and he used that wit to really convince people to do things,” Johnson said.

Ayotte recounted the day during the 2015 presidential campaign when Trump read aloud his then-rival Graham’s personal phone number at a televised campaign event. Shortly after, Graham went with Ayotte’s young family to watch “Minions.”

“So my son, who was probably 5 or 6 years old, Lindsey had him on the phone answering the calls, and so Jake would pick up the phone and say, ‘Oh, hey, who is this? Why are you calling?’” Ayotte said. “So we had a lot of laughs over that.”

Remembrances will continue at the South Carolina State House on Wednesday morning. Graham’s casket will be carried by a South Carolina State Guard horse-drawn military wagon, known as a caisson, followed by an F-16 flyover to mark his more than three decades in the Air Force and Air Force Reserve.
A funeral service, open to the public, will be held at First Baptist Church of Columbia. A private family burial will take place in Pickens County, where Graham was born and raised.

title: Nasdaq 100 slides into correction as global chip and memory stocks sell off
summary: Chip stocks around the world sold off sharply, the latest chapter in the months long jitters surrounding artificial intelligence, memory and chip stocks.
story: Chip stocks around the world sold off sharply on Tuesday, the latest chapter in the months long jitters surrounding artificial intelligence, memory and chip stocks.

The sell off briefly pushed the Nasdaq-100 index into correction territory, which is a drop of 10% or more from its most recent record high. The influential index tracks the top 100 non-financial companies traded on the Nasdaq exchange.
Shares of several chip and memory giants, including Sandisk, Western Digital, Seagate, Micron, and AMD all fell around 10% in early trading.
Dell Technologies, which produces servers that use chips and memory made by those firms, tumbled 13%. Intel shares slid 7%.
The selling kicked off overnight in Asia, with stocks traded on markets in Korea, Japan, and Taiwan.
Both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, the primary manufacturers of memory used in AI data centers, plunged more than 15%. Kioxia, another computer storage maker, plummeted 18%.
The latest wave of investor unease followed a report on Monday that a Chinese state-backed firm was beginning mass production of domestic chip-making tools.
However, the report did not name the company. NBC News was not able to verify the report.
Still, shares of established firms that make chip manufacturing equipment such as ASML, Canon and Nikon fell sharply on the news.

Tuesday’s moves also come ahead of major earnings reports later in the week from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and other companies that are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build AI data centers. Those results could prove pivotal to the trajectory of the market.

Last week, Alphabet shares plunged 7% after the company reported its own results and increased its projected capital expenditures to as much as $205 billion. Most of that will go to building and expanding data centers.
Evercore technology analyst Mark Mahaney said last week that Alphabet would likely set the stage for Microsoft and Amazon to do the same when they report this week.

“The Capex increase increases the odds of similar behavior from AWS and Azure,” he wrote in a note on Wednesday, referring to capital expenditures, or money companies spend on building physical infrastructure.
Still, despite investor jitters, “cloud demand appears relentless,” he added.
On Friday,  JPMorgan said that artificial intelligence-related spending by companies is set to approach “about $870bn by year-end 2026.” That’s 77% higher than the same spending a year ago.
So-called hyper scalers like Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, and Alphabet represent “about $750bn of that total,” said JPMorgan head of cross-asset strategy Fabio Bassi.

Apple, which is not spending hundreds of billions of dollars building its own data centers, rallied about 1% Tuesday to a more than $5 trillion market cap for the first time. Apple has also surpassed Nvidia as the world’s largest public company.
Nvidia shares were slightly higher mid-morning.
Beyond the rout in chip stocks, U.S. markets overall continued to power higher.
In mid-day trading, the S&P 500 traded higher, while the Russell 2000 was only slightly lower.
“Nothing seems to shake this market,” wrote HSBC’s Max Kettner in a Monday note.

Part of that has to do with positive earnings results so far this quarter. “Even when excluding the blockbuster numbers from Alphabet, the average earnings surprise is well in excess of the post-COVID-19 pandemic average,” he wrote.

title: Search for North Carolina woman Liz Waddell is still a missing person case, Grenada police say
summary: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
story: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, a 44-year-old Cary resident, was last seen going out for a swim at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

“At this time, the matter continues, continues to be treated as a missing person investigation,” acting Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught told reporters on Tuesday. “I repeat, at this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Surveillance cameras captured Waddell walking on a jetty near the water at 11:36 a.m. the morning she went missing, Connaught said.
She went into the water at 11:51 a.m. and more footage captured her swimming under the jetty at 12:04 p.m., the police official said.
Witnesses have told investigators they later saw Waddell in the open water, police said.
Waddell’s traveling partner was captured on surveillance cameras on the beach at 12:46 p.m. and she reported the swimmer missing to police at 5:50 p.m., Connaught added.
“There is nothing questionable about her account of the investigations and we continue to receive cooperation from her,”  Connaught said of the traveling companion.
Even though Waddell hasn’t been seen in nearly six days, police said they still seek to rescue her.
“It is our hope that Elizabeth will be found and found alive and well,” Connaught said. “The Royal Grenada Police Force remains equally hopeful that she will be safe and that she is safe.”
Local police had been appealing to fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to keep their eyes peeled for medium build woman with short blonde hair.
Waddell and her friend first arrived in Grenada, the island nation in the eastern Caribbean Sea that’s about 100 miles north of Venezuela, on July 11.
The missing woman’s husband has since come to the island to help in the search effort, officials said.

“Any bit of information will do at this time, and we do hope that we can locate Elizabeth very soon,” Connaught said. “Again, we empathize with the family, relatives, and friends, and we are hopeful that Elizabeth will be found alive. Thank you.”

title: Washington says goodbye to Sen. Lindsey Graham
summary: A special ceremony at the Capitol and a funeral service at the National Cathedral on Tuesday will be private, but both events will be livestreamed for the public.
story: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump, congressional colleagues and world leaders Tuesday will say their final goodbyes to Sen. Lindsey Graham, the influential and colorful foreign policy hawk whose sudden death this month at age 71 stunned Washington and reverberated in capitals around the globe.

Two days of ceremonies and funeral services began Tuesday morning when Graham’s American flag-draped casket arrived at the Capitol for a special ceremony in the rotunda — his last visit to a building where he served for more than three decades.

In honor of the senator’s long military career, an armed forces body bearer team slowly carried his casket up the Capitol steps. Graham served as an Air Force judge advocate general, or JAG, officer and retired from the Air Force Reserve in 2015 with the rank of colonel.

Senate colleagues, past and present, Cabinet members and Graham’s family and staffers packed the Rotunda. Among those paying tribute were former Sens. Bob Corker and Lamar Alexander, both Tennessee Republicans; Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Richard Burr, R-N.C.; Jeff Flake, R-Ariz.; Pat Toomey, R-Pa.; and Kelly Ayotte, now New Hampshire’s GOP governor.

“It’s such a loss in terms of his voice on foreign policy and America’s role in the world,” Ayotte, who traveled regularly with Graham on Senate trips around the world, told NBC News, adding: “He loved life, he had so much fun, and no one could make you laugh more than Lindsey Graham.”
Vice President JD Vance, who also served with Graham in the Senate, remembered the late senator’s “swashbuckling, infectious laugh” and called him a “true American original.”

Graham, Vance said, had a common touch, likely from his humble upbringing in western South Carolina, and could connect with all people, whether it was political leaders or the waitstaff in the Capitol.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

“Lindsey Graham loved people from all walks of life. … He was fascinated in the waitstaff in the Senate dining room. He was fascinated in the people who made the food. He was fascinated in the lowest staffer who had been hired three days earlier,” Vance said at the Capitol ceremony. “He was fascinated by, of course, the very leadership of our country, and I think he was fascinated in people because he loved people.”

Others on hand were former South Carolina Rep. Trey Gowdy, a Fox News host; acting Attorney General Todd Blanche; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former senator; and White House budget director Russell Vought.

“It’s difficult to believe that we’re here today to say a final farewell to Lindsey as he leaves the Capitol for the last time. My heart is heavy,” Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said at the ceremony.

“Lindsey was a towering figure here in the Senate and on the international stage. ... Lindsey will be remembered as a senator and as a statesman,” Thune said. “But for me, most of all, I will remember him as my friend. It’s hard to think that there will be no more Senate dinners with Lindsey.”

Graham’s sister and only sibling, Darline Graham, who was appointed to replace him in the Senate, walked tearfully up to the casket alone, then placed her hand on the casket. Backed by Trump, she is running for a full term in an Aug. 11 primary.
She was joined by her family. Then a parade of Trump officials, senators and Senate staffers paid tribute. Former Sen. Burr kissed the casket “to say goodbye.”
“He was one of our close friends,” Burr said.
From the Capitol, Graham’s casket departed for the Washington National Cathedral for an invitation-only funeral service at 2 p.m. ET. That will be livestreamed.

Trump is expected to speak at the funeral. Cabinet officials and congressional and military leaders are expected to be on hand, as are global leaders who viewed Graham as a key American ally on defense and foreign policy matters, including Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Graham didn’t come close to winning the presidency when he ran against Trump in 2016, but Tuesday’s send-off in the nation’s capital was fit for a president, with Trump, Vance and world leaders personally honoring Graham.
Graham did not lie in state or honor in the Capitol rotunda, but few other lawmakers have received such a ceremony.

It was a testament to Graham’s political influence and longevity. In addition to his 33-year military career, Graham had previously served as Senate Judiciary Committee chairman and was Budget Committee chairman when he died. He was also one of the most quoted members of Congress; he was a regular on Fox News and had logged 63 appearances on NBC’s “Meet the Press.”

“He’s been one of a kind, irreplaceable. dedicated his life to this country. I mean, in the end, gave his life to this country. I mean, all the arduous travel took a toll on him,” said Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who succeeded Graham as Budget chairman upon his death.
“Nobody had a quicker wit ... and he used that wit to really convince people to do things,” Johnson said.

Ayotte recounted the day during the 2015 presidential campaign when Trump read aloud his then-rival Graham’s personal phone number at a televised campaign event. Shortly after, Graham went with Ayotte’s young family to watch “Minions.”

“So my son, who was probably 5 or 6 years old, Lindsey had him on the phone answering the calls, and so Jake would pick up the phone and say, ‘Oh, hey, who is this? Why are you calling?’” Ayotte said. “So we had a lot of laughs over that.”

Remembrances will continue at the South Carolina State House on Wednesday morning. Graham’s casket will be carried by a South Carolina State Guard horse-drawn military wagon, known as a caisson, followed by an F-16 flyover to mark his more than three decades in the Air Force and Air Force Reserve.
A funeral service, open to the public, will be held at First Baptist Church of Columbia. A private family burial will take place in Pickens County, where Graham was born and raised.

title: Major earthquake rocks southern Japan, injuring dozens
summary: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate and prompting the collapse of several buildings, including a shopping mall.
story: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate and prompting the collapse of several buildings, including a shopping mall.
Japanese officials instructed roughly 300,000 people in the country’s southern Kumamoto prefecture to seek shelter at evacuation centers.

The Japan Meteorological Agency said the earthquake, with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 and depth of just over 6 miles, was at the highest end of the seismic intensity scale. Its epicenter was about 12 miles south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of around 700,000, according to officials.

The Japanese Cabinet Office’s disaster management division said the earthquake struck around 4:27 p.m. local time (3:27 a.m. ET), with a tsunami advisory issued for the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas minutes later. The warning was later lifted, state broadcaster NHK reported.

An unknown number of people were trapped in a shopping mall, according to fire officials, who said an explosion had been heard on the building’s second floor. Twenty to 30 mall employees were unaccounted for, NHK reported.

Commercial broadcaster TBS quoted local police as saying “quite a few” people are believed to have been killed after the explosion. A second broadcaster, Fuji TV, said that multiple deaths had been confirmed at the mall.

title: Michigan dad fatally shoots his wife and 6 kids before killing himself, authorities say
summary: The bodies were found Friday inside the Grand Haven residence, police said, and the children were 5 to 15 years old.
story: A man fatally shot his wife and their six children before he set the Michigan home they shared ablaze and turned the gun on himself, authorities said Monday.
Kristopher Karolkiewicz, 47, killed his wife, Amanda, 39, and their children, ages 5 to 15, Ottawa County Sheriff’s Capt. Jake Sparks said at a news conference.
They were found dead after first responders arrived at the home in Grand Haven, on the eastern shore of Lake Michigan, late Friday morning, Sparks said. Autopsies showed all had been shot, he said.
“The investigation at this point shows that this is a murder-suicide, with the fire being started after the murders,” Sparks said.
Four of the children were the couple’s biological kids, and two 11-year-old girls had been adopted, Sparks said, adding that the children’s identities would not be released at this time.
The Michigan State Police Fire Investigation Unit and a state police dog assisted the sheriff’s office with its investigation, State Police Lt. Pat Agema said by email.
Firefighters and police responded around 11:42 a.m. Friday after neighbors reported a house fire, Sparks said, and they found the bodies in different bedrooms.
“Preliminary indications are that the fire was intentionally set in numerous different places throughout the residence, in the interior of the home,” he said.
The violence may have started the night before and carried on into Friday morning, Sparks said, because there were earlier reports of the smell of smoke in the area.
Investigators believe Karolkiewicz used a registered handgun in the attack, Sparks said, but he wouldn’t say whether a firearm has been recovered from the fire-damaged residence.
Amanda Karolkiewicz was a substitute teacher, children’s book author and advocate for special needs children, NBC affiliate WDIV of Detroit reported.

“Our daughter Mandy was a kind and devoted soul who loved her family and her students,” her parents told WDIV. “We treasured every moment we had with her and her six children, and words cannot adequately express our devastation.”
Grand Haven Area Public Schools formally recognized Amanda this year as a dedicated substitute who “pours her heart into her work,” the station reported.
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 or go to 988lifeline.org to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline or visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources.

What causes boob sweat?

Boob sweat is caused by heat and moisture getting trapped in the skin fold between each breast and the chest, a.k.a. the underboob area. It’s a warm, closed-off  part of the body where heat and moisture can’t evaporate, so sweat easily builds up, says Madeline June, a board-certified nurse practitioner at The Well Westlake. Boob sweat can lead to uncomfortable rashes from chafing (irritation that happens when skin rubs on skin or clothing), or yeast and fungal overgrowth.

Experts told me that several factors exacerbate boob sweat, including high temperatures and humidity levels; hormonal changes, like those that happen during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause; and tight-fitting bras and clothes made from non-breathable fabric.
Can you prevent boob sweat?

No, you can’t completely prevent boob sweat, just like how you can’t completely prevent sweat on any part of your body. “It’s a common issue, not a hygiene failure, and most people experience it at some point,” says Courtney Coons, a board-certified nurse practitioner at PERK Plastic Surgery.
That said, you can use certain products and practice habits that help reduce boob sweat and prevent related skin irritation.

Some people are more prone to boob sweat than others, says June, including:

Those with larger breasts, which cause more skin-to-skin contact between the breasts and the chest, increasing how much heat and moisture gets trappedThose experiencing hormonal changes during menstruation, pregnancy, perimenopause and menopause, which can cause increased sweat production

Yes, boob sweat can cause rashes. They’re technically called intertrigo, a type of rash that develops in skin folds, like the ones between the breasts and the chest, says June.
There’s two types of boob sweat rashes to know about:

Heat rashes: When heat stays trapped in the skin fold, it often leads to chafing, which shows up as a raw, irritated rash from the constant friction, says Coons. Moisture rashes: When moisture stays trapped in the skin fold, it can lead to yeast or fungal overgrowth, which shows up as a red, itchy rash, says Coons.

Moisture rashes: When moisture stays trapped in the skin fold, it can lead to yeast or fungal overgrowth, which shows up as a red, itchy rash, says Coons.

To treat rashes from boob sweat, keep the affected area clean, dry and friction-free, says June. Also apply a barrier ointment like petroleum jelly (including Vaseline and Aquaphor) or a zinc oxide cream like Desitin to protect the skin. Topical steroids like hydrocortisone cream can help with itching and inflammation. By following this treatment plan, rashes usually heal within a few days of following this regime, says Coons.

If you don’t treat a rash right away, the irritated, inflamed skin can break down further, leading to open wounds that are more prone to infection, says Coons. Then, when those wounds heal, they can leave behind long-term skin discoloration — hyperpigmentation shows up as dark spots, while hypopigmentation shows us as light spots, says June.

It’s also important to know when to see a doctor about these rashes. Typical irritation presents as mild redness, itching or burning, and the skin is intact without drainage (clear fluid that leaks out of wounds), says June. If your rash isn’t getting better after a week of consistent at-home care, or it’s getting worse and you notice any of the following symptoms, it’s time to see a doctor as you could have an infection, says Coons: persistent redness, spreading redness, warmth, severe itching or burning, open sores with drainage, pain or odor. Your doctor can give you a prescription-strength treatment.

title: The best flats with arch support (that also look good)
summary: Flats look great but often don’t have arch support, leaving your feet unaligned and achy. Podiatrists share what to look for and the best supportive flats to shop now.
story: Flats are stylish and can certainly be more comfortable than heels, but they are not without their own issues. The problem often lies in the very name of this style of shoe. A completely flat shoe means no support — particularly arch support, which goes a long way when it comes to keeping your feet comfortable and stable.

“Arch support keeps your foot better aligned, which helps support your entire body and makes sure there is good distribution of pressure across your feet,” says Dr. Gregory Alvarez, a podiatrist at the Ankle and Foot Centers of America. That even distribution matters more than you might think — when weight isn’t spread properly across your foot, it puts extra strain further up the chain, in your muscles, ligaments and joints.

The good news is that there are flats out there that offer that much-needed arch support. To help you find flats that actually do right by your feet, I asked podiatrists what to look for and rounded up the pairs worth adding to your shoe rotation.

Podiatrists have previously recommended Birkenstocks to me as a go-to brand for walking sandals because they offer a supportive, contoured footbed with built-in arch support. These ballet flat-style shoes cradle your arch and heel the way most flats never do, plus have a strap that goes across the top of your foot to keep your foot from sliding around.
How I picked the best flats with arch support
To select the best flats with arch support, I asked experts what to consider while shopping. Here are the things they suggest you prioritize:

Support: Look for a raised section in the middle of your insole — almost like a mini hill. This will tell you that the shoe has built-in arch support. Additionally, look for a flat that cups your heel to keep your foot in place. This ensures your foot doesn’t move around and helps you stay steady on your feet. Limited bendability: Before you buy a pair of flats, consider trying a bend test. Here’s how to do it: Try bending the sole in half. You want it to be able to bend it at the ball of the foot, not at the midfoot, says Landau. Firmness from the midfoot to the heel means the shoe is more supportive, while bending at the ball gives you enough flexibility to be comfortable.Heel drop: You want your flats to be, well, flat — but too flat could cause issues. That’s where a heel drop comes in. Heel drop is the height difference between the heel and the forefoot of a shoe; you want the back of the shoe to be slightly more elevated than the front of the shoe. “This matches the foot anatomy more and reduces stress on your feet,” says Landau. “In turn, this will reduce pain and soreness.” That said, finding a decent heel drop in a flat can be difficult. Ideally, a heel drop between 7 and 10 millimeters is ideal — but you won’t find that in most flats. So, the experts I spoke with suggested aiming for 3 millimeters, which should be easier to find.

“Wearing flats that aren’t supportive can lead to pain in the arch, plantar heel, posterior heel and ball of foot,” says Landau. “It can also cause knee, low back and hip pain.” In turn, this can lead to conditions like achilles tendonitis and plantar fasciitis, which are inflammation issues that can cause ongoing pain.

Yes, you can absolutely add insoles to your flats. Many flats do not have arch support and there are plenty of insoles out there that do not take up too much room in sleeker styles of flats, says Landau, who says she often adds her own custom insoles to her flats.
