Harlan Coben, a thriller author whose adaptations are sweeping streaming platforms, and whose latest book is the memoir “Plot Twist”Julia Quinn of “Bridgerton” fameIsaac Fitzgerald, memoirist and author of “American Rambler”Yasmine Cheyenne, wellness expert and author of “The Comeback Era” John Searles, the former books editor at Cosmo and the author of “Single Girls”Brad Thor, author of thrillers set in the world of counterrorism including the latest “Choke Point”Emma Straub, a Read With Jenna author whose latest is “American Fantasy”Poet and author of children’s fiction Kwame Alexander, who also edited the poetry collection “This Is the Honey”
Harlan Coben, a thriller author whose adaptations are sweeping streaming platforms, and whose latest book is the memoir “Plot Twist”
Julia Quinn of “Bridgerton” fame
Isaac Fitzgerald, memoirist and author of “American Rambler”
Yasmine Cheyenne, wellness expert and author of “The Comeback Era”
John Searles, the former books editor at Cosmo and the author of “Single Girls”
Brad Thor, author of thrillers set in the world of counterrorism including the latest “Choke Point”
Emma Straub, a Read With Jenna author whose latest is “American Fantasy”
Poet and author of children’s fiction Kwame Alexander, who also edited the poetry collection “This Is the Honey”
Here are the books to try this year, ranging from romance to thriller and beyond.
July 2026
"The MASH Up" by Laurie Marie Meyers
A rom-com about a woman who wakes up on her 35th birthday and is trapped in a game she created as a teen.

What John Searles said: “For fans of ‘13 Going on 30’ comes Laura Marie Meyers’ sparkling and laugh-out-loud funny romantic comedy about a woman who wakes up the morning after her 35th birthday to find that she is trapped inside a game of MASH that she created in the 7th Grade. This hits the millennial sweet spot and is a fun read.”
"Dominion" by Jean Kwok
The first book apart of Kwok's new fantasy series.

What John Searles said: “‘Fourth Wing’ — by way of Chinese mythology — meets ‘The Hunger Games’ in a perilous world where a young woman with no memory and little magic may hold the key to uniting the Dominions and saving the mortal realm, the first in The Silk and Iron trilogy, from the New York Times bestselling author of Read With Jenna pick ‘Searching for Sylvie Lee’ and ‘Girl in Translation.’”
"Helpless" by Jessica Knoll
A woman who attends her college professor's funeral is kidnapped by her ex-boyfriend in this twisty thriller.

What John Searles said: “A successful Hollywood producer returns to her college alma mater and is reunited with her volatile, obsessive ex-boyfriend. What begins as an unsettling chance encounter spirals into a dark, twisty erotic thriller when Henry drugs and kidnaps her, forcing Faye to confront years-old secrets and the true, dangerous nature of their twisted past. Juicy and fun and full of twists.”
"The Odyssey" by Homer
The greek classic.

What John said: “It seems so surprising to me but the classic Greek poem we all had to study in college is being released as one of summer’s biggest movies, starring Anne Hathaway and Matt Damon and Tom Holland. Directed by Christopher Nolan, the film was shot entirely on IMAX cameras in breathtaking locations like Greece, Iceland and Italy. It stars Matt Damon as Odysseus, Anne Hathaway as Penelope, Tom Holland as Telemachus, and Zendaya as Athena.”
June 2026
"Phoebe Berman's Gonna Lose It" by Brooke Averick
A funny, warm story about a hopeless romantic determined to lose her virginity before her 30th birthday.

What Isaac Fitzgerald said: “‘Phoebe Berman’s Gonna Lose It’ is oh so warm and deeply charming — a novel about romance, friendship, anxiety, and the strange little deadlines we invent for becoming ourselves. In this case, well, losing one’s virginity before turning 30. Laugh-out-loud funny while still being tender and big-hearted, here is a love story in the truest sense, about learning to want honestly, messily and entirely on your own terms.”
"Main Characters: A Novel" by Bobby Palmer
A love story of a pair whose paths unexpectedly cross throughout two decades, told from outside perspectives.

What Isaac Fitzgerald said: “Main Characters’ is a brilliant book — a captivating love story told from the margins by the people who perhaps understand us before we understand ourselves. The book follows Clara and Seb across two decades as their lives brush up against one another’s, but is told from the perspective of everyone around them. A clever concept that totally works, here is a great summer read for anyone who has ever believed in the life-changing power of truly being seen.”
"This Vast Enterprise: A New History of Lewis & Clark" by Craig Fehrman
After years of research, this is an entertaining history of US history's two famous explorers.

What Isaac Fitzgerald said: “An incredible feat, Craig Fehrman’s ‘This Vast Enterprise’ is a wildly entertaining history of Lewis and Clark — the product of more than half a decade of rigorous and immensely impressive research — that never loses sight of the adventure at its center. Fehrman brings this legendary expedition thrillingly to life by turning our attention beyond Lewis and Clark themselves, revealing the oft-overlooked people and perspectives that made the journey possible. Expansive, compelling, and alive on every page, this is a perfect summer read for America’s 250th anniversary.”
"The Art of Loving You" by Natasha Bishop
The sequel to Bishop's "Only for the Week" of an intimate, spicy romance set during a bucket list road trip.

What Yasmine Cheyenne said: “Impossible to put down, this romance winds you through love, loss and the joy thats possible on the other side of change. If you love a plot that moves you as much as it inspires you, this is your pick!’
"Love by the Book: A Novel" by Jessica George
An honest story about the complications of adult friendships and new connections.

What Yasmine Cheyenne said: “A page-turner that puts words to what so many of us quietly feel about adult friendships — the growing pains, the unexpected shifts, and the beauty of who finds you in the in-between.”
"Waiting on a Friend: A Novel" by Natalie Adler
A story about friendship and community during a time of defiance and loss.

What Yasmine Cheyenne said: “A debut that somehow makes you feel more alive the deeper it pulls you into loss — an absolute love letter to a moment in history that still echoes today, with all the heart and humor to prove it.”
May 2026
"The Lost Book of Lancelot" by John Glynn

What Isaac Fitzgerald said: “This is a wildly entertaining retelling of the King Arthur myth, focusing on the life of Lancelot through a lense of queer exploration. Glynn does a fantastic job blending historical elements alongside adventure and fantasy. Filled with incredible world building, Glynn’s writing shines as he explores the Arthurian era with authority, and breathes new life into these long-known legends.”
"Famesick: A Memoir" by Lena Dunham

What Isaac Fitzgerald said: “’Famesick’ is the singular memoir from a singular voice — famously ‘a voice of a generation,’ as the line on her show ‘Girls’ goes — and polarizing figure in millennial culture, Lena Dunham. But you don’t have to be a GIRLS fan to enjoy this marvelous memoir. For starters, it’s rare to get a celebrity memoir this dishy and confessional, this genuinely shocking, sure. But also, you rarely if ever get them this well-written. You can feel how much care and craft went into this book, how much intelligence and skill, which is why it’s getting the response it’s getting, and why it is likely to stick around well past the news cycle.”
"Burnout Summer" by Jenna Ramirez

What Isaac Fitzgerald said: “’Burnout Summer’ follows the story of Camille Luna, a young woman who has just gotten out of a night in jail for some small crimes after losing her job and spiraling. Camille is picked up by an old friend, Danny, who whisks her off to his beachside hometown in Rhode Island, saving her for the summer from her flailing, corporate life in Washington DC. What ensues is an utterly spectacular will-they-or-won’t-they where the guy is delightfully straightforward and has his life together and the girl is the messy one. Ramirez’s sparkling writing makes the beach town come to life on the page — you can almost smell the sea salt in the air — a perfect blend of escapism and romance.”
April 2026
"Escape!" by Stephen Fishbach
Stephen Fishbach survived “Survivor” twice and wrote a novel inspired by his experiences. For Straub, a “Survivor” fan, this book is all a person could ask for.
“This is a novel about a reality TV program based on ‘Survivor.’ He’s a really smart, funny writer,” Emma Straub said.
"The Reservation" by Rebecca Kauffman

Emma Straub likens “Reservation” to “bingeing a whole season of ‘The Bear.’” It’s an “immersive novel” set over the course of one day at a small restaurant in a college town, she says. The headline news in the restaurant? John Grisham has made a reservation and everything needs to be perfect.
"The Fountain" by Casey Scieszka
Vera Van Valkenburgh has returned home for the first time in 128 years. After enjoying the fruits of the fountain of youth, Vera is tired and ready for a release.
“We need more contemporary novels with fantastical elements,” Emma Straub said. “This is a debut, smart and fun. Immortality in the Hudson Valley!”
"This Is Not About Us" by Allegra Goodman
Filled with humor, this is a story about growing old and the love that connects a family across generations.

How is it possible that an apple pie could cause a years-long rift between sisters? After Sylvia and Helen Rubinstein’s sister passes away, their relationship is in turmoil, enough so that a baked good could cause a major problem.
Coben calls this his “favorite novel of the year” so far.
"The Left And The Lucky" by Willy Vlautin
This text is an honest display of the power of friendship and how, in various ways, it can save our lives.

“The Left and the Lucky” is the latest from an author who is known for his portraits of contemporary American life. In this one, a young boy befriends his next-door neighbor, offering him an escape from his tumultuous family life.
Coben calls this book “gut-wrenching” and “compassionate,” with shades of John Steinbeck. There’s “dignity and integrity” in this working-class story, he says.
"Mad Mabel" by Sally Hepworth
Mad Mabel is a funny, inspiring, story of an underestimated woman about to prove everyone wrong.
At 15, Elsie Fitzpatrick became Australia’s youngest convicted murderer. Now 81, Elsie has left that behind her — until a young girl moves in across the road and unearths her past.
“Sally Hepworth is a huge star in Australia. This is the book that’s going to make her a huge star here,” Harlan Coben said on TODAY. He calls this book “funny, twisty and suspenseful.”
March 2026
"Imperfect Women" by Araminta Hall
This psychological thriller explores guilt, retribution, love and betrayal through three fascinating perspectives.

Nancy Hennessy is murdered and leaves behind a secret: The identity of a lover who nobody knew about. Not her husband. Not her friends. Not her daughter. The adaptation is soon to air on AppleTV+ starring Elisabeth Moss and Kerry Washington.
"Where the Wildflowers Grow" by Terah Shelton Harris
Be inspired by Terah Shelton Harris' newest story of survival and redemption.

“Where the Wildflowers Grow’ opens with a harrowing scene: A prison bus crashes over a ravine leaving only one survivor. Leigh survives and runs away to a flower farm in rural Alabama, starting a tale of hope and redemption.
"That's What Friends Are For" by Wade Rouse
Inspired by The Golden Girls, this hilarious story celebrates love, aging, and finding your people.

Fans of “The Golden Girls” will love this book inspired by the show about friendship and aging in style. Theodore Copeland’s estranged sister and her granddaughter show up at his oasis in Palm Springs, bringing secrets and disruption to his life with the “Golden Gays” (his nickname for his friend group).
"Python's Kiss: Stories" by Louise Erdrich
Explore Louise Erdrich’s writing with this magnificent collection of her stories.

Louise Erdrich, whose last book was chosen for Read With Jenna’s book club, has a new collection of short stories written from the past two decades of her storied career. According to the description from the publisher, the story collection features characters like “a tribal newsletter editor whose son tells her a story that nothing in her experience can encompass” and a girl who decides to spend her life with a stone.
February 2026
"And Now, Back to You" by B.K. Borison

What Julia Quinn said: “I’m not saying B.K. Borison has magic powers, but it’s a little suspicious that her romance novel about two meteorologists stranded together during the storm of the century is landing in bookstores right now... as half the country is clearing out from the storm of the century. Seriously though, ‘And Now, Back to You’ is simply delightful in every way. The characters are charming and real, and the book manages to make you laugh and tug on your heartstrings. Five stars, all the way.”
"Keeper of Lost Children" by Sadeqa Johnson

What Julia Quinn said: “I love when fiction introduces me to a piece of history I never knew about, and ‘Keeper of Lost Children’ does just that by shining a light on the true story of the ‘Brown Baby Plan,’ a 1950s movement spearheaded by African-American journalist Mabel Grammer to bring biracial children of white German women and Black American GIs to the United States for adoption.’ In Keeper of Lost Children,’ Mabel has been fictionalized as Ethel Gathers, who has moved to Germany with her husband, who is an officer in the US Army. She is shocked when she discovers hundreds of biracial babies living in German orphanages and, after adopting several children herself, begins a one-woman mission to find homes for the rest. I loved everything about this book, from the impeccably researched plot to the beautifully-drawn characters.”
"Project Hail Mary" by Andy Weir

What Julia Quinn said: “I loved ‘The Martian,’ both on page and screen, so it was a no brainer for me to pick this up. Andy Weir puts a lot of science in his science fiction, but he also spins a terrific story with compelling characters, including our protagonist, Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is somehow tasked with saving the world from a climate fueled apocalypse. Fortunately for humanity, Ryland soon teams up with Rocky, an alien life-form who’s a bit like a metallic spider (but with a heart of gold and a keen sense of sarcasm). The stakes in this novel are sky high, but Weir keeps the story grounded with geeky humor, and it’s easy to see why ‘Project Hail Mary’ is predicted to be one of the biggest blockbuster movies of 2026.”
"How to Commit a Postcolonial Murder" by Nina McConigley

What Julia Quinn said: “Every now and then I pick up a book solely because I’m intrigued by the title. What is a postcolonial murder? And why do I want to know how to commit one? Georgie Ayyar Creel is a 12-year-old Indian-American child, who, along with her sister Agatha, are navigating girlhood in a very white Wyoming town where ‘Indian’ usually means Native American. Their lives are upended by the arrival of their uncle Vinny, who emigrates from India with his family. Vinny molests them, repeatedly, and the two girls decide to poison him slowly with antifreeze. I thought this books would be a mystery, and in some ways it is, but is much more a tale of girlhood, and sisterhood, and all the ways a family bond can fracture. Georgie’s narration is wry and sharp, often speaking directly to the reader, and in this way, we are forced to reckon with her choices as if they were our own. ‘How to Commit a Postcolonial Murder’ is the kind of book that is difficult to describe, but so very easy to recommend.”
Quinn also shared a list of books she read and enjoyed for the rest of the year:

“And the Crowd Went Wild“ by Susan Elizabeth Phillips (February)“She Fell Away“ by Lenore Nash (March)“The Antiquarian’s Object of Desire“ by India Holton (April)“Annie Knows Everything“ by Rachel Wood (April)“The Paris Match“ by Kate Clayborn (April)“Anxietyland“ by Gemma Correll (April)“All We Have is Time“ by Amy Tordoff (June)“Game of Rogues“ by Julie Anne Long (June)“The Missed Connection“ by Tia Williams (June)
“And the Crowd Went Wild“ by Susan Elizabeth Phillips (February)
“She Fell Away“ by Lenore Nash (March)
“The Antiquarian’s Object of Desire“ by India Holton (April)
“Annie Knows Everything“ by Rachel Wood (April)
“The Paris Match“ by Kate Clayborn (April)
“Anxietyland“ by Gemma Correll (April)
“All We Have is Time“ by Amy Tordoff (June)
“Game of Rogues“ by Julie Anne Long (June)
“The Missed Connection“ by Tia Williams (June)
January 2026
"Behind These Four Walls" by Yasmin Angoe

What Brad Thor said: “Ten years after her best friend vanishes, a woman poses as a journalist to infiltrate the wealthy family connected to her disappearance. Every answer raises a worse question — was her friend a victim, or was she playing a deeper game?”
"Drive Me Crazy" by Lizzy Dent

What Brad Thor said: “Like an even steamier version of the Brad Pitt movie ‘F1.’ She’s an up-and-coming Formula 1 team principal. He’s her new hotshot driver — and her childhood crush — so their careers depend on working together without blowing up the team or each other. It’s high-speed romance with stakes you instantly get.”
"The Viper" by Brad Meltzer
What Brad Thor said: “A dying man hides something priceless inside the suit he plans to be buried in — then he’s murdered for it. It’s a killer premise with a personal gut-punch payoff!”
"People We Meet on Vacation" by Emily Henry

What Brad Thor said: “Best friends, polar opposites, years of summer trips — and the one question they’ve avoided: are they actually meant to be together? Read the book now, then watch the Netflix adaptation drop January 9. It’s your perfect ‘book first, binge next’ pick.”
"Mattering" by Jennifer Breheny Wallace

What Brad Thor said: “A lot of people don’t need another goal — they need to feel like they actually count. Mattering goes straight at the quiet stuff driving burnout and drift: feeling invisible, disconnected, and stuck on autopilot. Wallace lays out concrete ways to rebuild connection and purpose — so the New Year isn’t just a reset of your calendar, it’s a reset of your life.”

title: Darlene Love is Turning 85! Her Tips For Staying Forever Young
summary: Acclaimed soul singer and Christmas holiday icon Darlene Love has a gift for staying young. Here’s her longevity and health tips.
story: Acclaimed soul singer and Christmas holiday icon Darlene Love has a gift for staying young.

Love, who stopped by TODAY on July 24 to promote her upcoming documentary “Darlene Love: I Know Where I’ve Been,”  will be turning 85 years old on July 26. The songstress, who still continues to perform live, has opened up in the past about the many keys to her remarkably active lifestyle. But one of the most important secrets boils down to a particular mindset, she said on the show.
“You know what?” she told TODAY’s Al Roker, Dylan Dreyer and  Savannah Sellers. “I love life!”
Love also joked on the show that her youthfulness sometimes makes for awkward moments while out with family.
“I have a son who is 65,” Love said. “And they think they’re my boyfriends.”

The octogenarian has been lighting up the stage and screen for decades now. Born Darlene Wright, Love first got a taste of fame as a member of 1960s background vocals girl group The Blossoms. As part of the successful trio, Love sang with big acts like Elvis, Frank Sinatra, Dionne Warwick and many more. The three, which included Fanita James, and Jean King, even provided backing vocals to the Halloween hit “The Monster Mash.”

Love would go on to further make a name for herself with her 1963 classic “Christmas (Baby Please Come Home),” a track that is often in regular rotation around the holidays. Her extensive decadeslong body of work landed her a place in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2011.

Love’s talents extended to the silver screen as well. She played main character Roger Murtaugh’s wife, Trish, in the “Lethal Weapon” film series. She’s also graced the Broadway stage as Motormouth Maybelle in “Hairspray.”

The soon-to-be-85-year-old doesn’t appear to be slowing down, either. And she’s been known for not only her electrifying performances, but also for doing them in 6-inch stilettos. For the multi-hyphenate, she’s said her youthfulness has to do with several factors, including a whole lot of rest.

“Sleep a minimum of six to eight hours. Your rest is very important because this profession is very grueling,” Love told the Digital Journal in a 2025 interview ahead of her Christmas tour later that year. “They say our 90-minute set is equivalent of a man working eight hours; that’s the amount of energy we expel,”
She also underscores the importance of staying active.

“You have to take care of your body, and I’ve always done that,” Love told the Digital Journal. “Right now, I’ll be 84 in a few weeks, I get up at 5 a.m. five days a week and I do a kickboxing class.”
Love also told the outlet that sometimes, she even walks the length of the Mario M. Cuomo Bridge in Rockland County, New York, where she lives.
“You really do have to keep yourself active,” she said. “Even when you are not working, you can’t just sit around and do nothing.”
Love has said in the past, she’s just thankful to be able to continue to do what she loves — performing.

“I thank God every day for my health, the fact that I still have my voice 🎤, I can walk, talk, and move like I’m in my 40s (okay, maybe 50s 😄)” Love wrote in a social media post in celebration of her 84th birthday. “Whether it’s good genes, pure luck, or just taking care of myself, I’m not questioning it. I’m just grateful 🙏🏽”

title: Didi Conn, 75, Re-Creates Her Frenchy Outfit for ‘Grease’ Show
summary: Didi Conn, who played Frenchy in the movie “Grease,” made an appearance at “Grease: The Immersive Movie Musical” in London.
story: One of Rydell High’s most famous students has returned to the school.
Didi Conn, who played Frenchy in the classic 1978 movie “Grease,” made an appearance at the July 23 London performance of “Grease: The Immersive Movie Musical.”
Conn, 75, wore a Pink Ladies jacket and fought back tears while wiping her eyes when “Beauty School Dropout” was sung during the show.
The actor also shared her wisdom on how to be a Pink Lady in a video posted on the show’s Instagram page.
“In order to be a Pink Lady, you gotta act cool, you gotta look cool, and you gotta be cool ‘til death do us part,” she said.
“And, think pink! Pink is the color of love. Just think about if you’re ever feeling lonely, there’s a big, warm, cozy, fuzzy pink blanket of love just hugging you,” she added.
Conn also met the show’s director, Matt Costain, and some of the stars, who asked her if she had any advice about being a Pink Lady.
“No, just love each other. That’s all. We really loved each other, except for Rizzo,” she joked, alluding to the tough leader of the group, played in the movie by Stockard Channing.
“I’m blown away by this,” she added. “All of you are perfect.”
Conn, who would later star on the sitcom “Benson” and the children’s series “Shining Time Station,” may have gotten a sign that the role of Frenchy was meant to be.

“My agent said, ‘You gotta go looking like the character,’” she said in a June 30 Instagram video about her audition for the part. “And all I knew was that her name was Frenchy. I did know that she wanted to be a beautician. And I’m driving home and what do I see, but Frenchy’s Beauty Parlor.”
Conn said she stopped into the shop and treated herself to a new hairdo.

“And Little Frenchy, she did my hair with at least two cans of spray,” she recalled. “I had a big hairdo and I learned so much about beauty school. And when I went to the audition, I told them the story about Frenchy. They told me later, as soon as I opened my mouth I had the role. I didn’t know that.”

title: Chris Anne Affleck, Civil Rights Organizer And Mother of Ben and Casey Affleck, Dies at 83
summary: Christopher Anne Affleck, mother of Ben and Casey Affleck, died in June after a monthslong battle with a terminal illness, according to her obituary.
story: Christopher Anne Affleck, mother of actors Ben and Casey Affleck, died in June after a monthslong battle with a terminal illness, the family announced July 23. She was 83.

Affleck, a civil rights organizer and teacher, received her diagnosis in December 2025 and was given six months to live, according to her obituary in The Boston Globe. She passed just after being able to witness one of her biggest ambitions, according to the family.

“Her greatest wish after her diagnosis, however, was to live to see her grandson graduate high school,” the family wrote in the obituary. “She did so, attending with her family on May 31, 2026. She died peacefully, in her sleep, two days later.”
Affleck, who was born in New York City in 1942, spent 35 years as a public school teacher in Massachusetts, the obituary said.
“Every student, whether just arrived from Haiti or Cambridge upper crust, was a cherished citizen of her classroom republic, equal to each other and to herself,” the family wrote in the tribute.

A Harvard graduate, Affleck also spent a large part of her life involved in civil rights movements. During Freedom Summer — a 1964 summer initiative aimed at raising awareness around violence against the Black community and increasing voter registration and political participation — Affleck got involved, teaching literacy classes, according to the obituary. An active participant in 1960s counterculture, Affleck also marched against the Vietnam War, the tribute said.
The family wrote in the obituary that Affleck’s unique, revolutionary spirit was present in her life since childhood.
“From the beginning of her life, Chris made her unconventional name her own, foreshadowing both the personality and the practicality that would follow her to her death,” the obituary said.

Affleck, the commemoration said, grew up idolizing her stepfather Sam, who was a World War II veteran and a civil rights supporter. During her years at all-girls private school Nightingale-Bamford, Affleck “made the most of an elite education while remaining skeptical of the tightly cloistered world it represented,” the obituary said.

In one particular instance, the obituary said, a teacher had chastised Affleck for her criticism of Jim Crow — the laws and policies that enforced racial segregation primarily from 1877 to the mid-1960s — without hearing the “other side.”

“She slipped down to a payphone to ask Woolworth’s whether they really did turn Black customers away,” the family wrote, referencing the now-defunct chain retail store. “That was Chris: always willing to acknowledge that she might be wrong and never letting that uncertainty be an excuse for inaction.”
She also had a sense of humor, proudly wearing a typo from her first email address that dubbed her “Chritopher” and embraced it twenty years, the obituary said.
Later on, it was Affleck’s five grandchildren — Indiana, 22, Violet, 20, Atticus, 18, Fin, 17, and Sam, 12 — that became the “animating force” in her life, the family said in the obituary.
“Chris was suitably proud of her descendants’ achievements, but she was delighted when they questioned, defied, or cleverly engaged authority,” the tribute said.

Affleck, who retired in 2008, remained involved in advocacy and organizing. She volunteered on the Barack Obama campaign trail, the obituary said. Shortly afterwards, she traveled to Palestine and, upon her return, became an organizer with the coalition group Alliance for Water Justice in Palestine, the family wrote. She was also a founding board member of the Sustainable Cape Project in Truro, Massachusetts.
“When her granddaughter’s student activist group needed a space for trainings, she invited them to Truro and attended every single workshop herself, taking notes,” the obituary said.
Even after her diagnosis, Affleck continued her social justice work, the commemoration pointed out.
“She called her friend, Josh Laub, to take oral histories of his time as a principal in the South Bronx,” the obituary said.

Ben Affleck has previously opened up about his love for his mother, sharing in an interview with Vanity Fair that he and friend and fellow actor Matt Damon were intent on bringing their beloved moms to their first Academy Awards experience in 1998. While Ben Affleck said that some felt the moment was quite unique, he told the outlet that bringing his loved one to the Oscars felt like a natural choice.

“We were sitting next to our moms and we won, and we kind of hugged our moms,” Affleck told the magazine. “And I remember, how everyone had made such a big thing out of it. As if this was such a novelty.”
“And I remember thinking, being insecure, like, ‘Why? Why is it weird that we’re bringing our moms?’” he continued. “Like, ‘Who else do you think we would bring?’ You know what I mean?”
Affleck added that there was “nobody else that was going to go.”
“That was it. Of course our moms were gonna go,” he said. “That really was innocent and not faked.”
CORRECTION (July 24, 2026, 10 a.m.): An earlier version of this article misstated that Christopher Anne Affleck died at 82 years old. She was 83.

title: Chloe Kim Has 1 Request For Fans Who Take Photos With Her — And People Say It’s ‘So Real’
summary: If you ever take a photo with Olympic snowboarder Chloe Kim, make sure you do this one thing.
story: If you ever take a photo with Olympic snowboarder Chloe Kim, make sure you do this one thing.
The gold medalist had a message to fans who post photos of them together, asking that if they edit themselves, consider touching up her appearance, as well.
“If you are going to stop me for a photo and you’re gonna post it,” she begins in a TikTok. “Facetune me too, ‘K.”
She jokingly continued, “Stop just Facetuning yourself, looking all gorgeous and I’m next to you like ... don’t. That’s rude.”
Many people in the comments section couldn’t help but agree with Kim, including fellow athletes.
Gold medalist and gymnast Suni Lee wrote, “pls this is so real.” Tennis superstar Coco Gauff also commented, “so real.”
“10000% agree,” wrote Olympic figure skater Adam Rippon.
Other fans loved her humor, writing, “I freaking love you you’re hilarious,” “Stop your so funny,” “this took me OUT omg.”
Some also posted previous photos that they had taken with her, with one person noting that they “didn’t have to facetune us bc we’re already fab.”
Kim replied, “omg.”
One person, however, brought up Abby Lee Miller’s post when she altered Neil Patrick Harris’ face in a selfie — and he took notice.

Back in December 2025, the former “Dance Moms” star posted an airbrushed photo of herself with Harris after seeing him, as well as James Corden and Bobby Cannavale, perform in the Broadway play “Art.”
Miller shared individual photos of herself with each star, but it was the snap with Harris that made headlines and caught the actor’s attention.
“Ummm… what did you do to my face..?” Harris commented on Miller’s post.
She replied to his comment, explaining that her past cancer diagnosis is why she edits her photos.
“Burkitt Lymophona, 10 rounds of invasive chemo & a big birthday — so I’m sticking with the filters!” Miller wrote. “You sir — always look fabulous no matter what!!!”

title: Some People, Including Keke Palmer, Are Just Finding Out Oprah Winfrey’s Real Name
summary: Keke Palmer was shocked to find out that Oprah wasn’t Oprah Winfrey’s real name. The media mogul then shared her name’s origin story.
story: Oprah Winfrey is one of the few celebrities whose first name is so iconic they go by a mononym. But it turns out that the former television host was actually given a different name at birth.

The 72-year-old journalist appeared as a guest on the July 21 episode of the “Baby, This Is Keke Palmer” podcast where she spoke about the start of her career and her success. Host Keke Palmer began the interview by sharing a fun fact she heard about the original spelling of Winfrey’s name.
Palmer revealed that Winfrey’s name is really “Orpah.”
Winfrey confirmed the fact and said, “It was Orpah from the Bible. Ruth, first chapter, 14th verse.”
She added that her name stems from the biblical story involving Ruth and Naomi.
“You know, Ruth said, ‘Wherever thy goest, I will go.’ And then Orpah said, ‘I’m going back. I’m sorry. I can’t. Too long. The road’s too long,’’ Winfrey playfully explained.
She recalled that she wasn’t the one who decided to adjust the spelling of her name and that the change happened following a mishap shortly after she was born.

“Nobody knew how to spell it,” she continued. “So, it turned out on my birth certificate, it’s Orpah. Then people started calling me Oprah. So it’s just the difference between the P being before the R or after the R. So once they started with Oprah, that’s it.”
Although the switch occurred when she was a child, Winfrey revealed she didn’t discover the truth about her name until decades later.
“I didn’t learn until I was, like, probably 20 or something that, ‘Oh, this isn’t really my name,’” she shared.
Winfrey told Palmer that the original spelling of her name remains on her birth certification.
The story about the origin of Winfrey’s name has resurfaced over the years.

During a November 2005 episode of “The Oprah Winfrey Show,” she introduced a clip from 1983 that showed her talking about her name while auditioning for a morning show in Chicago, according to E! News.
In the clip, Winfrey said, “My name is Oprah Winfrey. Oprah, spelled O-P-R-A-H, and if you notice, it’s Harpo spelled backwards.”

She added, “My folks did not really like Harpo Marx. We did not even have a television set for a number of years. Originally, I was named from the Bible by Aunt Ida, who named me from Ruth, the first chapter at the 14th verse, Orpah. But no one knew how to spell in my home, and that’s why I ended up being Oprah.”
The mogul has also responded to a few X users for over a decade with the correct spelling and inspiration behind her name.
When journalist Yashar Ali celebrated Winfrey’s 64th birthday on X in 2018, he included her real name in the tweet, surprising some social media users in the comments.
In 2024, one X user learned the spelling error for the first time and expressed their disbelief in a tweet. The post reached over one million views.

More learned the truth following Palmer’s podcast. Beneath a clip of the conversation between Winfrey and Palmer, one comment read, “Imagine changing your name because people couldn’t pronounce it, then becoming one of the most famous people in the world.”
Another said, “Orpah realizing she got the better stage name by accident is kind of incredible.”

title: Oil prices slide as U.S. and Iran pause strikes to give ‘space’ for diplomacy
summary: The two sides halted fire over the weekend, following 13 nights of attacks that threatened new pain for the global economy.
story: Oil prices tumbled Monday as the United States and Iran paused their escalating strikes to make “space” for diplomacy.
The two sides halted fire over the weekend, following 13 consecutive nights of attacks that shattered their deal to end the war and threatened new pain for the global economy.
International oil benchmark Brent closed down by 8.7%, at $88.36 per barrel, while U.S. crude fell by 7.5% to $82.61 per barrel.
The moves were a sharp and rapid reversal from last week, when prices gained more than 9% and Brent rose as high as $102. Last week was oil’s third straight week of gains.

Prices fell to nearly their lowest levels of the day after President Donald Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that the U.S. was talking with Iran “right now.” He added that he was not in a rush to make a deal and had “plenty of time” for talks.

Stocks broadly rallied earlier in the day, but those gains faded as the day progressed. By late afternoon trading, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq were flat. The Dow still had a slight gain of about 200 points.
U.S. Treasury yields, which steer consumer borrowing rates, declined only slightly and were still near the highest level since early 2025.

The renewed optimism follows mounting fears of a return to all-out war across the Middle East, as the battle for control of the crucial Strait of Hormuz expanded to the Red Sea, another key waterway for global trade.
Iran has launched several drones at ships in the strait in the past several days, according to a U.S. official, who noted that the U.S. military shot down the drones and no ships were impacted.
Iranian-backed militias also continue to target U.S. interests, U.S. forces and partners in Iraq, the official said. The U.S. has also been defending against those attacks.
Trump said Thursday that he was considering a “massive attack” to try to break Iran’s grip on the strait, but since then the U.S. and Iran have refrained from attacks for three days.
The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, Mike Waltz, told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” on Sunday that the decision to halt strikes came in response to ongoing talks between the two sides.

“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” he said, adding that talks were “ongoing” but that there was “internal fighting” on the Iranian side.
Waltz dismissed reporting that U.S. weapons stockpiles are depleted.
Still, Tehran offered limited hope for any ramped-up peace efforts.

“Mediators may convey messages from the American side to us concerning regional developments, but at the present time we have no negotiations with the American side,” Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday at a news conference.
He said Tehran would “never allow America to determine the timing of war and peace” and would “continue to defend ourselves for as long as our interests and considerations require.”
Baghaei maintained that the Strait of Hormuz was “closed.”

Oil prices had soared above $100 per barrel last week for the first time in two months as the conflict spiraled, with Hormuz effectively blocked and new disruption from attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in the Red Sea.
Shipping traffic through Hormuz was limited over the weekend, with more activity visible through the Bab el Mandeb choke point.

Along the Strait of Hormuz, just 29 verified transits were recorded from Friday to Sunday, according to an NBC News analysis of MarineTraffic data. Activity fell from 12 crossings Friday to six Saturday, before increasing to 11 Sunday.
Traffic along Bab el Mandeb remained higher, with 100 verified crossings over the same period. Daily activity was broadly stable, with 35 crossings Friday, 31 Saturday and 34 Sunday.
Prior to the war, some 20% of the world’s oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz, with its repeated closure sending energy prices soaring and global markets tumbling throughout the conflict.
“The market seems to be forever seeking good news from an arena that really is not providing any,” PVM analyst John Evans said.

“A stay of military strikes might seem an improvement, but it does not come with any guarantees that oil will soon flow from the area. ... Prices will only continue lower if high prices once again dent demand, not questionable mini-ceasefires,” Evans said.

On Monday, the semiofficial Iranian Tasnim news agency reported that six vessels had attempted to pass through Hormuz “by switching off their navigation and position systems.” It said one of them “suffered an incident” while the others were returned to the Persian Gulf “under Iran’s decisive management.”

Jordan, a key U.S. ally, said it downed two drones early Monday, though it was not clear who launched them. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed drones fired by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
Meanwhile, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu made his way to Washington on Monday, with plans to discuss Iran in a meeting with Trump set for Tuesday.
“Our objective is to safeguard our security while also expanding the circle of peace around us,” Netanyahu said in comments prior to his departure.

He also noted that he was traveling to the U.S. to pay his final respects at the funeral of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., whom Netanyahu described as “one of the greatest friends Israel has ever had.”
Beyond the Middle East, attacks between Russia and Ukraine have also increasingly focused on shipping, adding another complication for markets.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine over the weekend of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, saying one sailor was killed and another injured. The ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Tehran in protest.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Kyiv had ‌noted Russia ⁠was passing on to Iran its satellite observations in the Middle East to enable Tehran to direct strikes in the region.

title: Mike Waltz dismisses concerns over depleted U.S. weapons stockpile amid Iran war
summary: The United Nations ambassador said the U.S. has “everything that it needs” for military operations against Iran.
story: Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” Sunday that the U.S. has “everything that it needs” for military operations against Iran, dismissing reporting that U.S. weapons stockpiles are depleted.

“I want to be crystal clear: The U.S. military, and I’ve verified this every which way, has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be,” he said. “And I have to tell you, the people that are leaking this nonsense deserve to be in jail.”

He was responding to questions about an NBC News report that U.S. military commanders are allowing some Iranian attacks through U.S. defenses as part of an effort to preserve the Pentagon’s weapons supply, according to two senior U.S. officials.
NBC News has also previously reported that U.S. weapons stockpiles are diminishing as the war with Iran continues.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Waltz initially argued that stockpiles were depleted during the Biden administration.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “inherited a depleted situation from not only Ukraine, but also the ongoing fight with the Houthis under the Biden administration and a depleted military under the Biden administration,” Waltz said.

The military under the Trump administration, he said, has decided that “one, they’re going to new types of munitions, cheaper munitions, new technologies, but also with these new defense budgets, rebuilding our great military.”
The White House and the Pentagon didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Hegseth appeared before lawmakers last week to ask for $67 billion in supplemental funding to expand production and speed up delivery of weapons.
During a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing in April, Hegseth acknowledged in an exchange with Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., that it could take “months and years” to rebuild the weapons stockpile.
In a separate interview with “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker, Kelly referred to that exchange, saying that the situation was “by their own making.”
“They’re not keeping track,” Kelly said. “They, at this point, this president and the people around him are incompetent.”
Asked whether he would vote to approve the supplemental funding, Kelly said he has not yet made a final decision.

“If we had some competent people running this department, you could figure out, how do you defend our nation in a way and give the troops what they need within a reasonable budget?” he said earlier. “What they’re asking for is not reasonable.”

In recent days, the U.S. launched nearly two weeks of consecutive nightly attacks on Iran. Trump has told reporters that the U.S. is still “talking to them,” but Iran and its proxies have continued strikes on ships, snarling global trading routes.
Asked whether Trump has decided against escalation amid the pause in consecutive strikes, Waltz said he “wouldn’t go that far at all,” adding that “the president is keeping all options on the table.”
“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” Waltz said. “Talks are ongoing; they’re happening at every level.”

On Saturday, a journalist for the French media outlet LCI reported that she asked Trump whether he was considering resuming full-scale war with Iran. She said Trump replied that “if we don’t get 100% of what we want, absolutely.”

title: Search for North Carolina woman Liz Waddell is still a missing person case, Grenada police say
summary: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
story: Grenadian police said Tuesday that their nearly week-old search for a missing North Carolina woman is still active, with hopes of finding the swimmer alive.
Elizabeth “Liz” Waddell, a 44-year-old Cary resident, was last seen going out for a swim at Grand Anse Beach on Wednesday, the Royal Grenada Police Force said.

“At this time, the matter continues, continues to be treated as a missing person investigation,” acting Commissioner of Police Randy Connaught told reporters on Tuesday. “I repeat, at this time, the matter continues to be treated as a missing person.”
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Surveillance cameras captured Waddell walking on a jetty near the water at 11:36 a.m. the morning she went missing, Connaught said.
She went into the water at 11:51 a.m. and more footage captured her swimming under the jetty at 12:04 p.m., the police official said.
Witnesses have told investigators they later saw Waddell in the open water, police said.
Waddell’s traveling partner was captured on surveillance cameras on the beach at 12:46 p.m. and she reported the swimmer missing to police at 5:50 p.m., Connaught added.
“There is nothing questionable about her account of the investigations and we continue to receive cooperation from her,”  Connaught said of the traveling companion.
Even though Waddell hasn’t been seen in nearly six days, police said they still seek to rescue her.
“It is our hope that Elizabeth will be found and found alive and well,” Connaught said. “The Royal Grenada Police Force remains equally hopeful that she will be safe and that she is safe.”
Local police had been appealing to fishermen, boat operators and residents along the southern coastline to keep their eyes peeled for medium build woman with short blonde hair.
Waddell and her friend first arrived in Grenada, the island nation in the eastern Caribbean Sea that’s about 100 miles north of Venezuela, on July 11.
The missing woman’s husband has since come to the island to help in the search effort, officials said.

“Any bit of information will do at this time, and we do hope that we can locate Elizabeth very soon,” Connaught said. “Again, we empathize with the family, relatives, and friends, and we are hopeful that Elizabeth will be found alive. Thank you.”

title: Major earthquake rocks southern Japan, injuring dozens
summary: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate and prompting the collapse of several buildings, including a shopping mall.
story: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake rocked southern Japan on Tuesday, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to evacuate and prompting the collapse of several buildings, including a shopping mall.
Japanese officials instructed roughly 300,000 people in the country’s southern Kumamoto prefecture to seek shelter at evacuation centers.

The Japan Meteorological Agency said the earthquake, with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 and depth of just over 6 miles, was at the highest end of the seismic intensity scale. Its epicenter was about 12 miles south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of around 700,000, according to officials.

The Japanese Cabinet Office’s disaster management division said the earthquake struck around 4:27 p.m. local time (3:27 a.m. ET), with a tsunami advisory issued for the Ariake and Yatsushiro seas minutes later. The warning was later lifted, state broadcaster NHK reported.

An unknown number of people were trapped in a shopping mall, according to fire officials, who said an explosion had been heard on the building’s second floor. Twenty to 30 mall employees were unaccounted for, NHK reported.

Commercial broadcaster TBS quoted local police as saying “quite a few” people are believed to have been killed after the explosion. A second broadcaster, Fuji TV, said that multiple deaths had been confirmed at the mall.

title: Berlin police kill suspect in Pride festival attack after manhunt
summary: Authorities say the 21-year-old was fatally shot after charging at officers with a knife, a day after an attack left one dead and 29 injured.
story: Berlin police shot and killed the suspect in this weekend’s deadly attack during the city’s Pride festival after he allegedly charged at officers with a knife while they tried to arrest him Sunday, authorities said.

The 21-year-old suspect was found at 6 p.m. local time at an allotment garden complex in the Spandau district, Berlin police said. Authorities said he rushed at members of the city’s special police unit, or SEK, with a weapon, prompting officers to open fire. Despite firefighters’ resuscitation efforts, he died at the scene.
Authorities have accused the suspect of driving a vehicle into a crowd and attacking people with a bladed weapon near Brandenburg Gate on Saturday night, killing a woman and injuring 29 others.
Three of the injured people have life-threatening injuries, Berlin’s fire department spokesman Dominik Pretz said Sunday morning, adding that eight are seriously injured.

Police identified the suspect as 21-year-old Abdul B., whom officials describe as a “radicalized” member of “Islamist circles” in Berlin. The country’s Interior Ministry later released the suspect’s last name, Ballout.
“Everything we are seeing here indicates that we have experienced an Islamist attack,” German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said at a news conference Sunday.

He identified the suspect as a German citizen of Lebanese background known to police after committing crimes in the past. Ballout had previously been sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison in Berlin, he said, which was commuted to parole.

He was sentenced for preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state and violating an enforceable prohibition under the Associations Act, the Office of the Berlin Public Prosecutor General said in a statement. The sentence was handed down in May.

The office said the verdict was based on information that he had attempted to travel to Syria last year to join the Islamic State group but was arrested in Lebanon, where he was in contact with several people he believed were members of the group and was sentenced to three months in prison, in part for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict. After that, the office said, he returned to Germany, was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and was held in pretrial detention until the verdict.

The office said the court found that he had “published prohibited IS propaganda on his Instagram account on June 16 and 24, 2024.” In determining the sentence, the court considered the three months he was held in Lebanon and the six months he spent in pretrial detention in Germany, the office said.

It also “took into account that Abdul B. had largely confessed during the trial, distanced himself from ISIS, and that there had been no concrete threat to protected legal interests,” the office said.

Before that, he had been convicted of assaulting someone at a Berlin high school in 2019, as well as robbing someone of a pair of headphones nearly a year later. He was also convicted in 2022 of assault and robbery by extortion, the office said.
Earlier this month, Berlin prosecutors searched his home for firearms but found only a toy gun, and the case was dismissed.
Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered in Berlin for one of Europe’s largest LGBTQ+ celebrations. The parade had passed through the park earlier Saturday.

The attack was outside the secure festival area, Dobrindt said, adding that many of those attacked were going to or from the festival site. A vehicle used in the attack was removed from the scene Sunday.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has condemned the incident in Berlin as “a heinous act.”
“They wanted us to treat each other with kindness and tolerance. This is an attack on our society,” he wrote on X, adding that the attack will be investigated with the “utmost severity.”
Saturday “should have been a day of joy, visibility and freedom,” Alfonso Pantisano, the Berlin state government’s queer liaison officer, wrote on social media.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed her sympathy to the victims Sunday, saying the Pride event stands for “freedom, dignity, and equality.”
“Every person should be able to live, love, and stand up for their rights without fear,” she wrote on social media.

title: U.S. forgoes strikes on Iran, but conflict in the Red Sea escalates
summary: U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that the pause in strikes was due to ongoing talks between the two countries.
story: The Iran war ​broadened over the weekend despite a pause in U.S. strikes, as Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Saudi oil installations along the Red Sea coast and Iran ‌accused Ukraine of targeting one of its vessels in the Caspian Sea.
The U.S. military said Saturday that its naval blockade against Iran “remains in full effect” but did not explain why it halted a streak of 13 nights of escalating strikes.
There were also no weekend reports of attacks by Iran on neighbors, similar to its daily rejoinders to the U.S. attacks.
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that a pause in strikes was due to ongoing talks between the two countries.
“What the president is doing right now, as we’ve seen all along, is giving some talks some space,” he said. “Talks are ongoing.”
Waltz added that while talks were ongoing at the highest levels of the Iranian and U.S. governments, there was “internal fighting” on the Iranian side.
“Some are seeking the guidance of the supreme leader,” he said. “Others want to move into a different direction, and that makes it hugely challenging.”
Iran ​will halt its own attacks as long as the United ⁠States maintains its pause on strikes, but Tehran remains skeptical of U.S. ⁠intentions, a ​senior Iranian source told Reuters on Sunday.

“Iran’s ⁠position remains ‘attack for attack’: ​if ⁠the attacks stop, ‌Iran will also halt its operations. That message ‌has already been conveyed ‌to the United States,” the source told Reuters, ⁠a day after Washington halted attacks following 13 successive nights of airstrikes.
“There is more skepticism than optimism about ‌the halt in attacks. ​The prevailing view ‌is that ⁠the pause is ⁠tactical rather than genuine,” the ‌source added.
Trump has decided, for now, to back away from plans to ramp up attacks on Iran, ⁠The New York Times reported Saturday, citing two people briefed on the discussion.

The president and his advisers, the newspaper said, have concerns about expanding the conflict, depleting ​defense stockpiles, alienating Middle East Gulf allies and affecting energy supplies and the global economy.

Vice President JD Vance and Gen. Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, ​both raised concerns about the U.S. munitions stockpile with Trump during a White House meeting on Friday, a U.S. official told CNN.
Operations are “on a hold,” a Department of Defense source told the broadcaster on Saturday.

Despite the Gulf lull, Saturday’s fighting between Iran’s Houthi allies and Saudi Arabia showed that the war, which has already disrupted energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz, could affect a second major ​shipping route and reignite Yemen’s civil war.
Separately, Iran’s Foreign Ministry accused Ukraine of attacking an Iranian commercial vessel in the Caspian Sea, saying one sailor was killed and another injured.
The ​ministry summoned Ukraine’s chargé d’affaires in Tehran to protest over an attack it described as “hostile and criminal,” state news agency IRNA said.

The Iranian denunciation coincided with comments by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy that Kyiv had ‌noted Russia ⁠was passing on to Iran its satellite observations in the Middle East to enable it to direct strikes in the region.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group struck sites belonging to Saudi state oil company Aramco in the cities of Jizan and Yanbu on Saturday.

A large column of smoke rose from the direction of the Aramco refinery in Jizan, near the Yemeni border, video on social media verified by Reuters showed. The refinery can process up to 400,000 barrels of crude oil ​daily.
Two Asia-based trading sources said they had been ​informed of potential damage to fuel ⁠and oil storage sites at Jizan. Aramco did not respond to requests for comment.

In Yanbu, two missiles aimed at oil installations were intercepted. Yanbu, Saudi Arabia’s main Red Sea oil port, has become a key route for Saudi oil skirting the Strait of Hormuz, ​which Iran has blockaded.

In Yemen, officials said the air force of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, which has ​opposed the Houthis for ⁠more than a decade, struck Houthi sites in the Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The officials said both sides in Yemen’s civil war were mobilizing forces along the front.
Saudi Arabia has led an Arab coalition battling the Houthis since the Iran-aligned fighters captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa.
The civil war, in which famine and fighting killed hundreds of thousands, has been paused by a ceasefire since ⁠2022.
But that ​truce broke down this month, with the Houthis effectively joining the wider war their Iranian allies have ​waged since being attacked by the United States and Israel five months ago.
The Houthis have declared a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia over the past week, and Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said all Saudi oil ​facilities could be targets.

title: ‘Cockroaches won’: India’s youth protest leaders declare victory as minister resigns
summary: India’s viral Cockroach Janta Party called off its nationwide protests Saturday after the country’s education minister resigned and the government agreed to a number of the activist movement’s demands.
story: India’s viral Cockroach Janta Party called off its nationwide protests Saturday after the country’s education minister resigned and the government agreed to a number of the activist movement’s demands.

Dharmendra Pradhan announced his resignation on X after talks with the CJP, which has demanded major reforms after the handling of an alleged exam paper leak triggered one of India’s biggest displays of public dissent in recent years, including one activist’s 26-day hunger strike.

“I hold deep respect for the aspirations, sentiments, and rightful expectations of the youth of this country,” Pradhan wrote on X. “Realising the dreams of India’s young generation has been the moral resolve of our political and social life.”

Ministers JP Nadda and Jitendra Singh later said at a news conference all police cases against protesters would be dropped and the government will pay compensation to the families of students who died by suicide after the alleged paper leaks, according to Reuters news agency. The government will also consider the CJP’s proposals for reforms to exams, the group said.

The CJP, a viral movement that began as an online parody of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, confirmed it had called off its protests because all of its major demands “have been accepted by the government.”
“Cockroaches won. Democracy won!” it said on X.
In New Delhi, crowds of students and activists were celebrating in the streets following the announcement, many of them waving Indian flags.
Prerna Vats, a 27-year-old Ph.D. student in Delhi who was among the crowds, said that as Pradhan’s resignation came, “everybody started hooting, shouting.”

“I think the government thought that the crowds would go down and they thought that we will feel even threatened when they unleashed violence on us via tear gas,” she said. Instead, she told NBC News, “there were more and more people, there were more and more volunteers.”
“I think when the students on Monday begin their semester, there will be this relentlessness and fearlessness that they will enter with, knowing full well that they’ve won something huge,” she added.
The scandal has been growing since May, when online leaks disrupted the NEET undergraduate exam, the fiercely competitive gateway to India’s medical schools.

Anger among India’s young people has exploded onto the streets in recent weeks, with protests spreading from New Delhi to other cities around the country, including Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad. Authorities have struggled to contain the growing protests, with police deploying tear gas and batons against the vast crowds close to the country’s Parliament building in New Delhi earlier this week.

The CJP, named after a remark from India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant comparing unemployed young people to “cockroaches,” became the center of what has been one of the biggest challenges to Modi in his 12 years in power.

As well as the minister’s resignation, protesters’ demands included compensation for the families of students who died by suicide after the exam paper leaks, and accountability over police suppression of their protests.
“Remember, do not mess with cockroaches,” it posted Saturday.
What's behind India’s Gen Z ‘cockroach’ movement

On Thursday night, Modi offered his first public comments in a video posted to Instagram. “I know the paper leak is not a trivial matter,” he said, announcing fast-track courts to prosecute cases involving examination paper leaks, while defending his government’s handling of the scandal.

But protesters said his response fell short of their demands for accountability and hundreds of people returned to the streets of New Delhi on Friday even as authorities shut 18 stations across the city’s metro network, disrupting a vital mode of transportation for its 23 million residents.

A 26-day hunger strike by activist Sonam Wangchuk had further galvanized the protests this week, after police forcefully admitted him to a hospital last weekend. He said in a post on X Friday that he ended his fast after appeals from dozens of members of Parliament and following “a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country.”
Wangchuk on Saturday called Pradhan’s resignation “a victory of peace, patience & perseverance.”
“Congratulations CJP, Gen Z of the nation and thank you all citizens for shedding fear and the fear of fear and rising up from every corner of the nation,” he posted on X.

title: U.S. launches new strikes and Trump threatens ‘massive attack’ as Iran widens war
summary: The United States launched a fresh barrage of strikes on Iran overnight as President Donald Trump threatened a major new escalation after Tehran opened a second front in its pressure campaign on the world economy.
story: JERUSALEM — The United States launched a fresh barrage of strikes on Iran overnight after Tehran opened a second front in its pressure campaign on the world economy.

President Donald Trump threatened a major new escalation and on Thursday told Axios he is weighing whether to launch a “massive attack” on the Islamic Republic that would be “bigger than ever before.” The president’s warning and subsequent 13th night of military strikes came as oil briefly surged above $100 a barrel.
Though Trump appeared to leave the door open for a diplomatic solution in comments to reporters on Friday afternoon.

“There’s two ways. I mean, it’s, you can just keep doing exactly what we’re doing and take them apart piece by piece. We could do it in a more rapid fashion, which we might do, or we can negotiate with them, which we’re also doing right now,” Trump told a gathering of reporters at the White House. “I mean, as we speak, we’re talking to them.”

Iran has shown little sign of bowing to U.S. demands, launching new attacks on shipping as well as U.S. bases and allies across the Middle East. These two fronts have combined to increase the cost of the renewed conflict — in human lives, including American soldiers, and global prices.
The struggle for control of the crucial Strait of Hormuz has now been extended to another key trade route, the Bab el Mandeb strait, after attacks by Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in the Red Sea.

And there were signs that some U.S. partners in the region may be losing patience. Senior Arab officials told NBC News they were growing frustrated with the threats, the daily escalations and the lack of diplomatic progress.

“We have no clue where this is going,” said one senior Arab official, with direct knowledge of regional developments. “It’s only getting crazier,” said another senior Arab official, directly involved with diplomatic efforts.

title: No basic services and nowhere to go: How Venezuelans are living a month after the earthquakes
summary: We visited the ruins of a housing complex built by the Chavista regime: the now homeless residents brave the heat, humidity, and flies from their tents, as they’re promised a house by 2027.
story: LA GUAIRA, Venezuela — A month has passed since earthquakes shook Venezuela and killed thousands, but in the state of La Guaira the old way of life feels like a distant memory.
Walking through a residential area is like passing through a graveyard of buildings that are no longer recognizable, not even for people who lived there for years.
And then there’s another reality affecting the state: the displaced. Hundreds of people are now living in donated tents after losing their homes.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
Some still hope the government will help them recover what they’ve lost. Others just want someone to tell them their house can be habitable again.
This is the case at the Brisas de Maiquetía housing development, located directly across from the international airport serving Caracas.

It’s a residential complex built under the Great Housing Mission, the state program created by the late President Hugo Chávez in 2011 to provide social housing to low-income individuals and disaster victims.
Upon entering, one observes a sea of ​​white and blue tarps beneath the once habitable buildings.
Ray Cazorla, a local resident who has lived there for almost 16 years, says the situation is getting worse every day and that the help that has arrived is extremely scarce.

“International aid is not being allowed to pass through here or it is not actually arriving [...] I saw publications showing a truck here with international boxes that were never delivered, it was a lie,” Cazorla told Noticias Telemundo.

The problem intensifies upon entering the tents. The heat, humidity, and steam make it impossible to stay inside. “We barely manage to survive like this. We survive thanks to fans that we had to connect to the power poles, with wiring that we installed ourselves,” Cazorla added.

Previously, residents slept in tents outside the housing complex, but when interim President Delcy Rodríguez visited the area on July 15 to inspect the relief efforts, they were told they had to return to the complex.

Inside, only bunk beds have been provided. Everything else — refrigerators, stoves, gas cylinders, even portable air conditioners— are possessions that families have managed to take from their apartments.

Cazorla explained that he has not been able to remove anything from his house because the stairs were badly cracked by the earthquakes and he fears that if he moves any heavy appliances, the staircase will give way completely.
According to him, the engineers who inspected the buildings said they have no structural problems, only issues with the masonry and brickwork. He doesn’t believe them.
“One of the towers has a broken main beam,” Cazorla said. “I don’t know if they’re going to repair it, but all the apartments are like that.”

Residents say that drinking water doesn’t reach the area. That’s why there are drinking water tanks with filters at various points throughout the development. They weren’t installed by the government, but by the Cadena Foundation, a humanitarian organization of the global Jewish community.
The filtration system, however, has flaws: filling a five-liter pot can take a whole day, since the process works drop by drop.
The remaining tanks — many salvaged from the ruins themselves — are filled with water from the street. Residents say it’s yellow water, unfit for drinking. They only use it for bathing and cooking.
“Every day we feel more alone. The first day the government arrived with a huge crowd, a real commotion, because we thought they were going to make the process quick,” Cazorla said.

Hopes faded when in the following days, he said, no one from from the government showed up and the neighbors were left alone, taking care of their homes and waiting in tents for the nightmare to pass.

The Venezuelan interim government assured them that they could return to their apartments by March 2027. The news wasn’t well received, although some have already resigned themselves to the idea that this tent will be their home for many months. “We’re going to be here for several months; we’re all living on the floor because nobody wants to leave their apartment for fear of having their few valuables stolen,” one person pointed out.
Some people have decorated the entrance to their tents with potted plants, flowers, and family mementos. Others are putting cement underneath them so the soil won’t bother them as much.

Brisas de Maiquetía has not been spared from looting, a problem affecting all of La Guaira. Some buildings have messages painted on their walls: “It’s already been looted” or “Neighbors, be alert, no more looting.” The residents said they themselves had  managed to control the situation, despite having a police post within the area and National Guard troops patrolling.
10 showers for 600 families

The area is home to more than 3,000 people, who must use the public restrooms provided by the state, many of which are poorly maintained. There are 10 public showers that have become unusable over time due to misuse by some residents.
A young couple who lived in the buildings said that they had to repair the showers themselves and are taking point on maintaining them so they’re usable.
“Now there’s no water because the children come unsupervised and use up the whole tank. By the time you go to take a bath, there’s none left,” one of them said.
Cazorla pointed to other daily issues and dangers.
“There are many mosquitoes, many flies. We are prone to the proliferation of cholera or dengue,” he said. “There is stagnant water from the rains and a viral outbreak could occur at any moment.”

Nora Romero, another neighbor, said that some people rush up to their apartments to shower, risking further collapse. The residents are trying to make a living in the ruins because living in the tents isn’t feasible, but the fear is constant: what will happen if an aftershock destroys the buildings?

“The situation is very delicate because there are children. They haven’t even cleared the rubble — we have received some aid, but what we need most is water for the children because diarrhea, flu, and coughs are already an issue,” Romero said.
“We are vulnerable. The stairs have already lost their foundations and are prone to collapse with any aftershock,” said Cazorla.
Rebuild what was broken

Carlos, who prefers not to share his last name, lives on the first floor of one of the towers. His apartment no longer has a kitchen or bathroom, but he and his two children still try to make a life for themselves among the ruins.
“I had just remodeled the apartment. I changed the kitchen, the flooring. Now I’ve lost all of that,” he said. The renovations cost around $2,000, money he knows he won’t get back.

Andrea Debur, who lives on the second floor of the buildings near the entrance to the housing development, said that only the ground floor and first floor apartments — the most affected — will be repaired, while the upper floors, which also suffered some infrastructure damage, were left without a response.

“Officials came to take pictures and then left. They built two walls, and both collapsed. These apartments are uninhabitable; the walls crack more every day,” said Debur, who lives in a tent with her partner, Leonexis Sequeda, and their daughter.
Aid has been scarce. The water from the tanks tastes like chlorine, so they choose to buy water or wait for the donated water to run out before drinking the one from the tanks.
Andrea said that following the earthquake, when they were living outside the housing development on a street across from the airport, they never lacked food.

That changed when Delcy Rodríguez visited the area on July 15th and they were relocated within the housing complex. “Since we’ve been here, they haven’t brought any food. They give us a  government bag, and we get everything else ourselves.”

Debur worked at the airport, which has not yet resumed operations, and is afraid to return. “Without a job, what are we going to do? We’re not saying we’re going to take advantage of the government, but they should help us.”
“It’s so depressing, we want to leave, but the question is where to go? The whole state has been affected. Businesses, supermarkets, pharmacies, banks — there’s nothing left,” Debur said.

According to residents, the governor of La Guaira state, José Alejandro Terán, has visited the neighborhood only twice, but the assistance has not been felt. We contacted the governor’s office for comment, but received no response.

Debur and Sequeda worry about the return to school and work. “I don’t know what condition the high school will be in. I’ve thought about going back to work, but I’m afraid, because all those structures are broken. If we go in there and they don’t fix it properly, there’s going to be another tragedy.”

The residents of Brisas de Maiquetía say they’re asking for only one thing: help. They’re asking the government to address the basic needs of the community and for the international community not to turn a blind eye.
Aside from rubble and collapsed buildings, the earthquake left behind people, who hope they won’t be forgotten.
An earlier version of this story was first published in Noticias Telemundo.

title: ‘Cockroach’ protests spread across India as leading activist ends hunger strike
summary: An activist has ended his 26-day hunger strike that galvanized India’s “Cockroach” protests, turning them into one of the biggest challenges to the government.
story: An activist has ended his 26-day hunger strike that helped to galvanize India’s youth-led “Cockroach” protests, turning them into one of the most sustained challenges to the country’s leadership in years.

But demonstrators vowed Friday to press on despite Sonam Wangchuk’s decision to end his fast, as the protests spread from New Dehli to other cities around the country including Mumbai, Hyderabad, Bengaluru and Ahmedabad.

Wangchuk’s fast began amid protests for education reforms after alleged leaks in some of the country’s most competitive university entrance exams, but quickly became a lightning rod for public anger over education, economic inequality and the rule of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Wangchuk said in a post on X that he ended his fast after appeals from dozens of members of Parliament and following “a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country.” Conceding that not all his demands were met, he said two federal lawmakers were present when he finished.
However, Abhijeet Dipke, a Boston University graduate and founder of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP), said the protests will continue until India’s Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigns.

“After all of this, we don’t accept anything less than a resignation,” he told supporters on Friday as protests showed no sign of dying down. CJP leaders have said they started talks with government officials at a neutral venue, raising hopes of a breakthrough in the standoff.

The CJP began as a satirical youth political movement after India’s Chief Justice Surya Kant compared unemployed young people to “cockroaches.” But the movement has soared in popularity and mounted the biggest challenge to Modi in his 12 years in power.
On Thursday night, Modi offered his first public comments, posting a video on Instagram addressing the young protesters and concerns about the exam paper leaks.
“I know the paper leak is not a trivial matter,” he said in his video. He also defended his government’s decision to let 2 million students retake medical entrance exams.
He also announced fast-track courts would prosecute cases involving examination paper leaks.

But protesters said his response fell short of their demands for accountability and hundreds of people returned to the streets of New Delhi on Friday even as authorities shut 18 stations the city’s metro network, disrupting a vital mode of transportation for its 23 million residents.

title: Oil prices surge to $100 per barrel after Red Sea attacks
summary: European and U.S. crude oil both jumped, hitting their highest levels in weeks.
story: Oil prices rose Thursday to their highest levels in nearly two months after the latest Iran war escalation threatened severe new disruptions to global energy supplies.

Brent crude oil, one of two key global benchmarks, closed higher by 7%, at $100.69 per barrel. Earlier in the trading day, it rose as high as $102 per barrel. That is its highest level in eight weeks, since the end of May.
U.S. crude oil also jumped for a second straight day, closing higher by 6.2%, at $92.19 per barrel — its highest close since June 4.
The prices surged after Tehran-backed Houthi rebels claimed attacks on two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea following their announcement of a naval blockade on the kingdom.
More on Iran war from NBC News

Trump enters an uncertain moment in Iran war that threatens to become a quagmireThat sinking feeling: Iranians feel the strain as Trump ramps up war again over HormuzThe costs of the Iran war are rising as Trump and Tehran signal no letup in the expanding conflict
Trump enters an uncertain moment in Iran war that threatens to become a quagmire
That sinking feeling: Iranians feel the strain as Trump ramps up war again over Hormuz
The costs of the Iran war are rising as Trump and Tehran signal no letup in the expanding conflict
It appeared to be the first time since the Iran war began that ship attacks had spread beyond the vicinity of the Strait of Hormuz, opening up a new front in the volatile conflict.
The Houthi threat is so unsettling to oil markets because millions of barrels per day pass through the Bab el-Mandeb strait to reach global markets.
About 12% to 15% of global maritime trade worth more than $1 trillion transits the waterway every year.
